questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: Which condition must hold for a relation \( R \) on a set \( A \) to be called reflexive?
options: \( \forall a \in A,\ (a, a) \in R \)
\( (a, b) \in R \implies (b, a) \in R \)
\( (a, b) \text{ and } (b, c) \in R \implies (a, c) \in R \)
There exists some \( a \in A \) such that \( (a, a) \in R \)
questions.explanation:
Reflexivity requires that \( (a, a) \in R \) for every single element \( a \in A \), with no exceptions.

A relation that contains \( (a,a) \) for only some elements is not reflexive on the whole set.
questions.hint: Reflexivity is about every element of \( A \), not just one.
distractor_logic: This is the definition of symmetric, not reflexive.
This is the definition of transitive, not reflexive.
Reflexivity requires the pair \( (a,a) \) for every element, not just some element.

questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: Let \( A = \{1, 2, 3\} \) and \( R = \{(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (1,2)\} \). Is \( R \) reflexive on \( A \)?
options: No, because \( (1,2) \) is an extra pair
Yes, because \( (1,1), (2,2), (3,3) \) are all present in \( R \)
No, because \( (2,1) \) is missing
Cannot be determined without knowing if \( R \) is symmetric
questions.explanation:
The set \( A = \{1,2,3\} \), so reflexivity requires \( (1,1), (2,2), (3,3) \in R \).

All three diagonal pairs are present in \( R \), so \( R \) is reflexive. The extra pair \( (1,2) \) does not affect this.
questions.hint: Check whether \( (a,a) \) is present for every \( a \in A \).
distractor_logic: An extra pair beyond the diagonal does not violate reflexivity; only a missing diagonal pair does.
Reflexivity only requires pairs of the form \( (a,a) \); it says nothing about \( (2,1) \).
Reflexivity is checked independently by scanning for \( (a,a) \) pairs; it does not depend on symmetry.

questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: Let \( A = \{1, 2, 3\} \) and \( R = \{(1,2), (2,1), (2,3)\} \). Is \( R \) symmetric on \( A \)?
options: Yes, because \( (1,2) \) and \( (2,1) \) are both present
No, because \( (1,1) \notin R \)
No, because \( (2,3) \in R \) but \( (3,2) \notin R \)
Cannot be determined without checking transitivity first
questions.explanation:
Symmetry requires that for every \( (a,b) \in R \), the reverse \( (b,a) \) is also in \( R \).

Here \( (1,2) \in R \) and \( (2,1) \in R \), which is fine. But \( (2,3) \in R \) while \( (3,2) \notin R \), so \( R \) is not symmetric.
questions.hint: Symmetry must hold for every pair, not just some of them.
distractor_logic: Checking only one pair is not enough; symmetry must hold for every pair in \( R \), and the pair \( (2,3) \) fails it.
Symmetry never requires diagonal pairs; that condition belongs to reflexivity.
Symmetry is checked directly from the pairs of \( R \) and does not depend on transitivity.

questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: Let \( A = \{1, 2, 3\} \) and \( R = \{(1,2), (2,3), (1,3)\} \). Is \( R \) transitive on \( A \)?
options: No, because \( (2,1) \notin R \)
No, because \( (1,1) \notin R \)
Cannot be determined since \( R \) is not reflexive
Yes, because the only chain \( (1,2), (2,3) \) gives \( (1,3) \), which is present
questions.explanation:
The only chain in \( R \) is \( (1,2) \) and \( (2,3) \), which requires \( (1,3) \in R \).

Since \( (1,3) \in R \), this chain is satisfied, and there are no other chains to check, so \( R \) is transitive.
questions.hint: Look for every chain \( (a,b), (b,c) \in R \) and check that \( (a,c) \) follows.
distractor_logic: Transitivity never requires reversed pairs; that concern belongs to symmetry, not transitivity.
Transitivity does not require diagonal pairs; that condition belongs to reflexivity.
Transitivity is an independent property and can hold even when \( R \) is not reflexive.

questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: Let \( A = \{1, 2, 3, 4\} \) and \( R = \{(1,1), (2,2), (3,3)\} \). Which single pair must be added to \( R \) to make it reflexive on \( A \)?
options: No pair needs to be added; \( R \) is already reflexive
questions.explanation:
Since \( A = \{1,2,3,4\} \), reflexivity requires all of \( (1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (4,4) \in R \).

Only \( (4,4) \) is missing from the given \( R \), so adding it makes \( R \) reflexive.
questions.hint: Reflexivity needs \( (a,a) \) for every element of \( A \), including \( 4 \).
distractor_logic: Reflexivity needs a diagonal pair for the element \( 4 \), not a pair connecting \( 4 \) to a different element.
This is also not a diagonal pair, so adding it does not fix the missing reflexive pair for \( 4 \).
Element \( 4 \in A \) has no pair \( (4,4) \) in \( R \), so \( R \) is not yet reflexive.

questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: Let \( A = \{1, 2\} \) and \( R = \{(1,1), (1,2), (2,1), (2,2)\} \). Is \( R \) symmetric on \( A \)?
options: No, because \( (1,1) \) and \( (2,2) \) should not both appear
Yes, because for every pair \( (a,b) \in R \), the pair \( (b,a) \) is also in \( R \)
No, because \( R \) contains four pairs instead of two
Cannot be determined without checking reflexivity first
questions.explanation:
The pairs are \( (1,1), (1,2), (2,1), (2,2) \).

The reverse of \( (1,2) \) is \( (2,1) \), which is present; the diagonal pairs are trivially their own reverses. So \( R \) is symmetric.
questions.hint: List each pair and confirm its reverse is also listed.
distractor_logic: Diagonal pairs are always their own reverse, so their presence never breaks symmetry.
The number of pairs is irrelevant to symmetry; only whether each reverse pair is present matters.
Symmetry is verified directly from the listed pairs and does not require reflexivity to be checked first.

questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: Let \( A = \{1, 2, 3\} \) and \( R = \{(1,2), (2,3)\} \). Which pair is missing for \( R \) to be transitive on \( A \)?
questions.explanation:
The chain \( (1,2) \in R \) and \( (2,3) \in R \) forces the requirement \( (1,3) \in R \) for transitivity.

Since \( (1,3) \) is absent, adding it is exactly what is needed to make \( R \) transitive.
questions.hint: Trace the chain \( a \to b \to c \) and identify which pair \( (a,c) \) it demands.
distractor_logic: The chain \( (1,2), (2,3) \) requires the pair \( (1,3) \), not its reverse \( (3,1) \).
Adding this pair does not satisfy the chain formed by \( (1,2) \) and \( (2,3) \); it introduces a different chain instead.
This is a diagonal pair relevant to reflexivity, not the pair needed to close the chain \( (1,2), (2,3) \).

questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: Let \( A = \{1, 2, 3\} \) and \( R = \{(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (1,2), (2,1)\} \). Which property does \( R \) satisfy among reflexive, symmetric and transitive?
options: \( R \) is reflexive only
\( R \) is symmetric only
\( R \) is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
\( R \) is reflexive, symmetric and transitive
questions.explanation:
All diagonal pairs \( (1,1),(2,2),(3,3) \) are present, so \( R \) is reflexive.

The reverse of \( (1,2) \) is \( (2,1) \), and both are present, so \( R \) is symmetric.

Every chain through \( 1 \) and \( 2 \) closes correctly (e.g. \( (1,2),(2,1) \Rightarrow (1,1) \)), and \( 3 \) only chains to itself, so \( R \) is also transitive.
questions.hint: Check each property against every relevant pair or chain before combining conclusions.
distractor_logic: \( R \) also satisfies symmetry, since the reverse of every pair, such as \( (1,2) \) and \( (2,1) \), is present, and it also satisfies transitivity.
\( R \) also satisfies reflexivity, since \( (1,1), (2,2), (3,3) \) are all present, and it also satisfies transitivity.

Checking every chain, such as \( (1,2) \) with \( (2,1) \) giving \( (1,1) \), and \( (2,1) \) with \( (1,2) \) giving \( (2,2) \), shows every required pair is already present, so transitivity does not actually fail.

questions.question: A relation \( R \) on a set \( A \) is called an equivalence relation when it satisfies which combination of properties?
options: \( R \) is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, all three together
\( R \) is reflexive and symmetric only
\( R \) is symmetric and transitive only
\( R \) is reflexive and transitive only
questions.explanation:
An equivalence relation is defined as a relation that is simultaneously reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

Dropping any one of the three properties means the relation is no longer called an equivalence relation, even if the other two hold.
questions.hint: All three defining properties must hold together — none can be skipped.
distractor_logic: Transitivity is also required; reflexive and symmetric alone are not sufficient to call \( R \) an equivalence relation.
Reflexivity is also required; a relation can be symmetric and transitive yet still fail to be reflexive.
Symmetry is also required; reflexive and transitive alone are not sufficient to call \( R \) an equivalence relation.

questions.question: Let \( A = \{1,2,3\} \) and \( R = \{(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2),(2,1),(2,3),(3,2),(1,3),(3,1)\} \). Is \( R \) an equivalence relation on \( A \)?
options: No, because \( R \) is missing a diagonal pair
Yes, since \( R \) is reflexive, symmetric and transitive
No, because \( (1,3) \) has no matching reverse pair
Cannot be determined without a Cayley table
questions.explanation:
All diagonal pairs are present, so \( R \) is reflexive.

Every pair's reverse is also listed, so \( R \) is symmetric.

Since every element relates to every other element, every chain closes, so \( R \) is transitive. All three hold, so \( R \) is an equivalence relation.
questions.hint: Check reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity in turn against the full pair list.
distractor_logic: All three diagonal pairs \( (1,1),(2,2),(3,3) \) are present, so reflexivity does hold.
The reverse \( (3,1) \) is present in \( R \), so symmetry is not violated here.
Reflexive, symmetric and transitive can be checked directly from the listed pairs; no table is needed.

questions.question: Let \( A = \{1,2,3\} \) and \( R = \{(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2)\} \). Why is \( R \) not an equivalence relation on \( A \)?
options: \( R \) fails to be reflexive, since \( (2,2) \notin R \)
\( R \) fails to be transitive, since \( (1,1) \notin R \)
\( R \) fails to be symmetric, since \( (1,2) \in R \) but \( (2,1) \notin R \)
\( R \) satisfies all three properties, so it is an equivalence relation
questions.explanation:
Reflexivity holds since all diagonal pairs are present.

But \( (1,2) \in R \) while \( (2,1) \notin R \), so symmetry fails.

Since even one property fails, \( R \) cannot be an equivalence relation, regardless of whether transitivity holds.
questions.hint: Check each property in turn; one failure is enough to disqualify \( R \).
distractor_logic: \( (2,2) \) is actually present in \( R \), so reflexivity is not the property that fails here.
\( (1,1) \) is present in \( R \), and there is no chain in \( R \) that is left unclosed, so transitivity holds.
The pair \( (1,2) \) has no matching reverse pair \( (2,1) \) in \( R \), so symmetry genuinely fails.

questions.question: The equivalence class of an element \( a \in A \) under an equivalence relation \( R \) is defined as which set?
options: \( [a] = \{x \in A : (a, x) \notin R\} \)
\( [a] = \{x \in A : x \neq a\} \)
\( [a] = \{a\} \) always
questions.explanation:
By definition, \( [a] = \{x \in A : (x, a) \in R\} \): it is the set of all elements of \( A \) that are \( R \)-related to \( a \).

Because \( R \) is reflexive, \( a \) itself is always in \( [a] \), but other elements may join it too.
questions.hint: The equivalence class collects every element related to \( a \), using the relation \( R \).
distractor_logic: This describes elements NOT related to \( a \), which is the complement of the equivalence class, not the class itself.
This is simply every element other than \( a \), which ignores the relation \( R \) entirely.
The equivalence class can contain more elements than just \( a \) itself, depending on which elements are related to \( a \) under \( R \).

questions.question: Let \( A = \{1,2,3,4\} \) and let \( R \) be the equivalence relation \( \{(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(4,4),(1,2),(2,1),(3,4),(4,3)\} \). What is the equivalence class \( [1] \)?
questions.explanation:
We need every \( x \) such that \( (x,1) \in R \).

\( (1,1) \in R \) and \( (2,1) \in R \), while \( 3 \) and \( 4 \) have no pair with \( 1 \). So \( [1] = \{1,2\} \).
questions.hint: Collect every element \( x \) with \( (x,1) \in R \).
distractor_logic: This misses \( 2 \), which is related to \( 1 \) because \( (2,1) \in R \).
This wrongly includes \( 3 \) and \( 4 \), which are not related to \( 1 \) under this \( R \); they form a separate class.
This is the equivalence class of \( 3 \) (or \( 4 \)), not of \( 1 \).

questions.question: Using the same \( A \) and \( R \) as above (\( A=\{1,2,3,4\} \), \( R = \{(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(4,4),(1,2),(2,1),(3,4),(4,3)\} \)), how many distinct equivalence classes does \( R \) create on \( A \)?
questions.explanation:
The related pairs show \( 1 \) and \( 2 \) form one class, \( \{1,2\} \), and \( 3 \) and \( 4 \) form another, \( \{3,4\} \).

Together these two classes partition all of \( A \), so there are exactly 2 distinct equivalence classes.
questions.hint: Group elements that are mutually related; each group is one class.
distractor_logic: This would mean all four elements share one class, but \( 1 \) and \( 3 \) are not related, so they cannot be in the same class.
Grouping \( \{1,2\} \) and \( \{3,4\} \) accounts for all four elements in exactly two classes, not three.
This treats every element as its own separate class, ignoring that \( 1,2 \) are related and so are \( 3,4 \).

questions.question: For any equivalence relation \( R \) on a set \( A \), the collection of all distinct equivalence classes always forms which structure on \( A \)?
options: A subset of \( A \) containing only one element
An ordered list of the elements of \( A \)
A partition of \( A \) — the classes are non-empty, pairwise disjoint, and their union is \( A \)
A relation identical to \( R \) itself
questions.explanation:
Because \( R \) is reflexive, every element lies in some class.

Because \( R \) is symmetric and transitive, two classes are either identical or completely disjoint. So the distinct classes partition \( A \).
questions.hint: Recall the standard partition property of equivalence classes.
distractor_logic: A single equivalence class can contain many elements; the full collection of classes is what spans all of \( A \).
Equivalence classes are unordered sets of elements, not a sequence or ordering of \( A \).
The classes are sets of elements, not a set of ordered pairs, so they are a different object from \( R \).

questions.question: Let \( A = \{1,2,3\} \) and let \( R \) be the equivalence relation \( \{(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,3),(3,1)\} \). Do \( 1 \) and \( 2 \) belong to the same equivalence class?
options: Yes, because both \( 1 \) and \( 2 \) are elements of \( A \)
Yes, because \( R \) is an equivalence relation and all equivalence relations have exactly one class
Cannot be determined without checking transitivity again
questions.explanation:
Since \( (1,2) \notin R \) and \( (2,1) \notin R \), elements \( 1 \) and \( 2 \) are not related.

So \( [1] = \{1,3\} \) and \( [2] = \{2\} \) are different classes; \( 1 \) and \( 2 \) do not share a class.
questions.hint: Two elements share a class exactly when they are related under \( R \).
distractor_logic: Simply belonging to \( A \) does not put two elements in the same class; only being related under \( R \) does.
An equivalence relation can produce several distinct classes; here it produces two, not one.
Transitivity has already been used to build \( R \); the classes can be read off directly from the given pairs.

questions.question: Which condition defines a one-one (injective) function \( f : A \to B \)?
options: \( f(x_1) = f(x_2) \implies x_1 = x_2 \)
\( \forall y \in B,\ \exists x \in A \text{ such that } f(x) = y \)
\( x_1 = x_2 \implies f(x_1) = f(x_2) \)
\( f(x_1) \neq f(x_2) \text{ for all } x_1, x_2 \in A \)
questions.explanation:
Injectivity is the statement \( f(x_1) = f(x_2) \implies x_1 = x_2 \): equal outputs can only come from equal inputs.

Equivalently, no two different elements of \( A \) are allowed to map to the same element of \( B \).
questions.hint: One-one means distinct outputs force distinct inputs — think of it as no two inputs sharing an output.
distractor_logic: This is the definition of onto, not one-one.
This direction always holds for any function by definition and does not capture injectivity.
This wrongly demands every pair of distinct or even equal inputs give different outputs, which is not the correct injectivity condition.

questions.question: Let \( A = \{1,2,3\} \), \( B = \{a,b,c,d\} \), and \( f(1)=a,\ f(2)=b,\ f(3)=c \). Is \( f \) one-one?
options: No, because \( d \in B \) has no pre-image
Yes, because \( 1, 2, 3 \) all map to distinct elements \( a, b, c \)
No, because \( |A| \neq |B| \)
Cannot be determined without knowing \( f^{-1} \)
questions.explanation:
The outputs are \( f(1)=a,\ f(2)=b,\ f(3)=c \), and \( a, b, c \) are all different.

Since no two distinct elements of \( A \) share an output, \( f \) is one-one.
questions.hint: Injective just means: do any two different inputs share an output?
distractor_logic: Having an unused element in \( B \) affects onto-ness, not one-one-ness.
Different sizes of \( A \) and \( B \) do not by themselves prevent \( f \) from being one-one; here all outputs are still distinct.
Injectivity is checked directly from the mapping by comparing outputs, with no need to find an inverse first.

questions.question: Let \( A = \{1,2,3\} \), \( B = \{a,b,c,d\} \), and \( f(1)=a,\ f(2)=b,\ f(3)=c \). Is \( f \) onto?
options: Yes, because every element of \( A \) has an image in \( B \)
Yes, because \( f \) is one-one
No, because \( d \in B \) has no pre-image in \( A \)
Cannot be determined without checking transitivity
questions.explanation:
The image of \( f \) is \( \{a,b,c\} \), but \( B = \{a,b,c,d\} \).

Since \( d \) has no element of \( A \) mapping to it, \( f \) is not onto.
questions.hint: Onto requires every element of the codomain \( B \), not just of \( A \), to be covered.
distractor_logic: That every input has an output is true of any function; onto requires every element of the codomain to be hit, and \( d \) is not.
Being one-one does not guarantee onto; here \( f \) is one-one yet still fails to be onto because \( d \) is left out.
Transitivity is a property of relations on a single set, not relevant to checking whether a function is onto.

questions.question: Let \( A = \{1,2,3\} \), \( B = \{a,b\} \), and \( f(1)=a,\ f(2)=b,\ f(3)=a \). Which pair of elements shows that \( f \) is not one-one?
options: No such pair exists; \( f \) is actually one-one
questions.explanation:
Here \( f(1) = a \) and \( f(3) = a \), so two distinct elements of \( A \) share the same image.

By definition, this means \( f \) is not one-one, with \( 1 \) and \( 3 \) as the violating pair.
questions.hint: Look for two different inputs producing the same output.
distractor_logic: These two elements have different images, \( a \) and \( b \), so this pair does not break injectivity.
These two elements also have different images, \( b \) and \( a \), so this pair does not break injectivity either.
The elements \( 1 \) and \( 3 \) both map to \( a \), which is a genuine violation of injectivity.

questions.question: Let \( A = \{1,2,3\} \), \( B = \{a,b\} \), and \( f(1)=a,\ f(2)=b,\ f(3)=a \). Is \( f \) onto \( B \)?
options: Yes, because both \( a \) and \( b \) have a pre-image in \( A \)
No, because \( f \) is not one-one
No, because \( 1 \) and \( 3 \) both map to \( a \)
Cannot be determined since \( |A| > |B| \)
questions.explanation:
The image set is \( \{f(1), f(2), f(3)\} = \{a, b, a\} = \{a, b\} \), which equals all of \( B \).

Since every element of \( B \) is hit at least once, \( f \) is onto.
questions.hint: Check whether every element of \( B \) appears as an output, regardless of repeats.
distractor_logic: One-one and onto are independent properties; a function can fail to be one-one and still be onto, as it is here.
Two elements sharing an image affects one-one-ness, not whether every element of \( B \) is covered.
The relative sizes alone do not decide onto-ness; the actual images must be checked, and here they cover all of \( B \).

questions.question: Which condition defines an onto (surjective) function \( f : A \to B \)?
options: \( f(x_1) = f(x_2) \implies x_1 = x_2 \)
\( \forall y \in B,\ \exists x \in A \text{ such that } f(x) = y \)
\( \exists y \in B \text{ such that } \forall x \in A,\ f(x) = y \)
\( \forall x \in A,\ \exists y \in B \text{ such that } f(x) = y \)
questions.explanation:
Surjectivity is the statement that for every \( y \in B \), some \( x \in A \) exists with \( f(x) = y \).

In other words, the image of \( f \) must be the whole of \( B \), leaving no element of \( B \) unused.
questions.hint: Onto means every element of the codomain \( B \) is hit by something in \( A \).
distractor_logic: This is the definition of one-one, not onto.
This wrongly demands a single output value for every input, describing a constant function, not surjectivity in general.
This is automatically true for any function, since every input must have some output; it does not capture the requirement that every element of \( B \) is covered.

questions.question: Let \( A = \{1,2\} \) and \( B = \{a,b,c\} \). Can any function \( f : A \to B \) be onto?
options: Yes, if \( f \) is chosen to be one-one
Yes, as long as \( f(1) \neq f(2) \)
No, because \( A \) has fewer elements than \( B \), so at least one element of \( B \) must be left without a pre-image
Cannot be determined without knowing the exact rule for \( f \)
questions.explanation:
Each element of \( A \) produces exactly one output, so at most \( |A| = 2 \) distinct elements of \( B \) can ever be covered.

Since \( |B| = 3 > 2 \), some element of \( B \) is always left without a pre-image, so no such \( f \) can be onto.
questions.hint: Compare the sizes of \( A \) and \( B \) directly.
distractor_logic: Being one-one does not add extra outputs; with only 2 inputs, at most 2 elements of the 3-element \( B \) can ever be covered.
Even with distinct images, only 2 of the 3 elements of \( B \) get covered, so one element of \( B \) is always left out.
The conclusion follows purely from counting: 2 inputs can never cover 3 required outputs, regardless of the specific rule.

questions.question: Let \( A = \{1,2,3\} \), \( B = \{a,b,c\} \), and \( f(1)=a,\ f(2)=b,\ f(3)=c \). Is \( f \) bijective?
options: No, because \( f \) is one-one but not onto
No, because \( f \) is onto but not one-one
Cannot be determined without finding \( f^{-1} \) first
Yes, because \( f \) is both one-one and onto
questions.explanation:
The outputs \( a, b, c \) are all distinct, so \( f \) is one-one.

Every element of \( B = \{a,b,c\} \) is covered, so \( f \) is also onto. Both hold, so \( f \) is bijective.
questions.hint: Bijective requires both properties together: one-one and onto.
distractor_logic: Every element of \( B \) — namely \( a, b, c \) — does have a pre-image, so \( f \) is in fact onto as well.
All three outputs \( a, b, c \) are distinct, so \( f \) is in fact one-one as well.
Bijectivity is checked directly by confirming one-one and onto; the inverse is only defined afterward, once bijectivity is established.

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: For functions \( f : A \to B \) and \( g : B \to C \), how is the composition \( (g \circ f)(x) \) defined?
options: \( (g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x)) \)
\( (g \circ f)(x) = f(g(x)) \)
\( (g \circ f)(x) = g(x) \cdot f(x) \)
\( (g \circ f)(x) = f(x) + g(x) \)
questions.explanation:
By definition, \( (g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x)) \): first \( f \) is applied to \( x \), and then \( g \) is applied to that result.

The order is read right to left, opposite to how it is written.
questions.hint: In \( g \circ f \), the function written second (\( f \)) acts first.
distractor_logic: This applies \( g \) first and \( f \) second, which is the reverse order from what \( g \circ f \) means.
Composition is not multiplication of the two function values; it is applying one function to the output of the other.
Composition is not the sum of the two function values; it is applying one function to the output of the other.

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: Let \( A=\{1,2,3\} \), \( f(1)=2, f(2)=2, f(3)=3 \), and \( g(1)=3, g(2)=1, g(3)=1 \), both functions \( A \to A \). What is \( (g \circ f)(1) \)?
options: \( g(3) \), left as \( 1 \) without identifying it as the final simplified value
questions.explanation:
First compute \( f(1) = 2 \).

Then compute \( g(2) = 1 \). So \( (g \circ f)(1) = g(f(1)) = g(2) = 1 \).
questions.hint: First apply \( f \) to \( 1 \), then apply \( g \) to that result.
distractor_logic: This is \( f(1) \) alone; the composition also requires applying \( g \) to that result.
This is \( g(1) \), which is part of computing \( (f \circ g)(1) \) instead of \( (g \circ f)(1) \).
This restates part of the correct computation without recognizing it as the final answer.

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: Using the same \( f \) and \( g \) as above (\( f(1)=2,f(2)=2,f(3)=3 \) and \( g(1)=3,g(2)=1,g(3)=1 \)), what is \( (f \circ g)(1) \)?
options: Same as \( (g \circ f)(1) \), since composition order never matters
questions.explanation:
First compute \( g(1) = 3 \).

Then compute \( f(3) = 3 \). So \( (f\circ g)(1) = f(g(1)) = f(3) = 3 \), which differs from \( (g\circ f)(1) = 1 \) found earlier — confirming composition order matters.
questions.hint: For \( f \circ g \), apply \( g \) first, then \( f \).
distractor_logic: This is the value of \( (g \circ f)(1) \), the composition in the opposite order, not \( (f \circ g)(1) \).
This is \( f(1) \) alone, not the result of first applying \( g \) and then \( f \).
Composition is generally not commutative; here \( (f\circ g)(1) = 3 \) while \( (g\circ f)(1) = 1 \), so the two genuinely differ.

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: When is the inverse function \( f^{-1} \) of \( f : A \to B \) meaningfully defined?
options: Whenever \( f \) is one-one, regardless of whether it is onto
Whenever \( f \) is onto, regardless of whether it is one-one
For every function \( f \), an inverse always exists
Only when \( f \) is bijective, i.e. both one-one and onto
questions.explanation:
If \( f \) is not one-one, \( f^{-1} \) would have to send some \( y \) to two different values, which is not allowed for a function.

If \( f \) is not onto, some \( y \in B \) would have no image under \( f^{-1} \) at all. So \( f^{-1} \) is defined only when \( f \) is bijective.
questions.hint: Both properties — one-one and onto — are needed together for an inverse to exist.
distractor_logic: If \( f \) is not onto, some elements of \( B \) have no pre-image, so \( f^{-1} \) cannot be defined on all of \( B \).
If \( f \) is not one-one, some element of \( B \) would have to map back to more than one element of \( A \), which is not a valid function.
An inverse function exists only when \( f \) is bijective; a function that is not injective or not surjective has no true inverse function.

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: Which of these correctly distinguishes the inverse function \( f^{-1}(x) \) from the reciprocal \( \dfrac{1}{f(x)} \)?
options: \( f^{-1}(x) \) is the function that reverses \( f \), satisfying \( f(f^{-1}(x)) = x \), while \( \dfrac{1}{f(x)} \) is simply one divided by the value \( f(x) \)
They are always equal for every function \( f \)
\( f^{-1}(x) \) exists only when \( \dfrac{1}{f(x)} \) is undefined
\( \dfrac{1}{f(x)} \) is defined only for bijective functions, just like \( f^{-1}(x) \)
questions.explanation:
\( f^{-1}(x) \) is defined so that applying \( f \) to it returns \( x \); it requires \( f \) to be bijective and is found by reversing the rule of \( f \).

\( \dfrac{1}{f(x)} \) is just arithmetic division by the output value and needs no bijectivity at all. Confusing the two is a classic error.
questions.hint: Reversing a function is a completely different operation from taking a reciprocal of its value.
distractor_logic: In general \( f^{-1}(x) \neq \dfrac{1}{f(x)} \); treating them as equal is a common but incorrect assumption.
There is no such relationship between the existence of \( f^{-1} \) and the reciprocal being undefined; the two concepts are unrelated in this way.
The reciprocal \( \dfrac{1}{f(x)} \) is defined simply wherever \( f(x) \neq 0 \); it has no connection to \( f \) being bijective.

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: Let \( A = \{1,2,3\} \) and \( f : A \to A \) be given by \( f(1)=2,\ f(2)=3,\ f(3)=1 \). Since \( f \) is bijective, what is \( f^{-1}(2) \)?
questions.explanation:
We need \( x \) with \( f(x) = 2 \).

Since \( f(1) = 2 \), it follows that \( f^{-1}(2) = 1 \).
questions.hint: Find the input \( x \) such that \( f(x) = 2 \).
distractor_logic: This confuses \( f^{-1}(2) \) with the input value \( 2 \) itself rather than finding which input produced the output \( 2 \).
This value would be \( f^{-1}(1) \), not \( f^{-1}(2) \); the pairing has been mismatched.
This treats \( f^{-1}(2) \) as a reciprocal, \( \dfrac{1}{f(2)} \), rather than the correct inverse-function value.

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: Continuing with \( f(1)=2,\ f(2)=3,\ f(3)=1 \) on \( A=\{1,2,3\} \), what is the complete mapping table for \( f^{-1} \)?
questions.hint: Reverse every arrow of \( f \): if \( f(a)=b \), then \( f^{-1}(b)=a \).
distractor_logic: This simply repeats the table of \( f \) itself rather than reversing each arrow.
This assumes \( f^{-1} \) is the identity function, which is only true if \( f \) itself were the identity; here \( f \) is not.
The middle entry is wrong: since \( f(3)=1 \ne 2 \), \( f^{-1}(2) \) cannot be \( 2 \); it must trace back to the actual input that produced output \( 2 \).

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: Let \( A=\{1,2,3\} \), \( f(1)=2,f(2)=3,f(3)=1 \), and \( g(1)=3,g(2)=1,g(3)=2 \). Checking \( (g \circ f)(x) \) for every \( x \in A \) shows it equals \( x \) each time. What does this confirm?
options: \( f = g \), since both are functions from \( A \) to \( A \)
\( f \) and \( g \) are both non-bijective
Nothing can be concluded without also checking \( (f \circ g)(x) \)
\( g = f^{-1} \), since \( g \circ f \) is the identity function on \( A \)
questions.explanation:
The defining property of an inverse is \( f^{-1}(f(x)) = x \) for all \( x \in A \).

Since \( g(f(x)) = x \) holds for every \( x \in A \), \( g \) plays exactly the role of \( f^{-1} \), confirming \( g = f^{-1} \).
questions.hint: An inverse pair satisfies \( g(f(x)) = x \) for every \( x \).
distractor_logic: Being functions on the same set does not make them equal; here \( f \) and \( g \) send \( 1 \) to different values, \( 2 \) and \( 3 \) respectively.
The opposite is shown: \( g \circ f \) being the identity is only possible because both \( f \) and \( g \) are bijective.
For finite functions between sets of the same size, one side of the identity check, together with bijectivity, is already enough to conclude \( g = f^{-1} \).

questions.question: How is a binary operation \( * \) on a set \( A \) formally defined?
options: \( * : A \times A \to A \), a rule assigning to every ordered pair \( (a,b) \) a unique element \( a * b \in A \)
\( * : A \to A \), a rule assigning to every element of \( A \) another element of \( A \)
\( * : A \times A \to \mathbb{R} \), a rule producing a real number from every pair
\( * : A \times A \to A \times A \), a rule producing a new pair from every pair
questions.explanation:
By definition, \( * : A \times A \to A \) takes an ordered pair \( (a,b) \) with \( a, b \in A \) and produces a single element \( a * b \), which must itself lie in \( A \).

This last requirement is called closure.
questions.hint: A binary operation combines two elements of \( A \) and returns one element, still inside \( A \).
distractor_logic: This describes a plain function on \( A \), not a binary operation, which must take a pair of elements as input.
A binary operation on \( A \) must land back inside \( A \) itself, not necessarily inside \( \mathbb{R} \).
A binary operation must output a single element of \( A \), not another pair.

questions.question: Let \( A = \{1,2,3\} \) and let \( * \) be defined as \( a * b = \max(a,b) \). What is \( 2 * 3 \)?
questions.explanation:
The operation is defined as \( a * b = \max(a,b) \).

So \( 2 * 3 = \max(2,3) = 3 \).
questions.hint: Apply the stated rule directly: take the larger of the two numbers.
distractor_logic: This would be \( \min(2,3) \), not \( \max(2,3) \), which is the operation actually defined here.
This treats \( * \) as ordinary addition, \( 2+3 \), rather than the maximum operation that was defined.
This treats \( * \) as ordinary multiplication, \( 2 \times 3 \), rather than the maximum operation that was defined.

questions.question: Let \( A = \{1,2,3\} \) and \( a * b = \max(a,b) \). Is \( * \) commutative on \( A \)?
options: No, because \( 2 * 3 \neq 3 * 2 \)
Cannot be determined without checking associativity first
Yes, because \( \max(a,b) = \max(b,a) \) for every pair \( a, b \)
No, because \( * \) has no identity element
questions.explanation:
Since \( \max(a,b) \) does not depend on the order in which \( a \) and \( b \) are written, \( a*b = \max(a,b) = \max(b,a) = b*a \) for every choice of \( a, b \in A \).

So \( * \) is commutative.
questions.hint: Compare \( a*b \) with \( b*a \) using the definition of \( * \).
distractor_logic: In fact \( 2*3 = \max(2,3) = 3 \) and \( 3*2 = \max(3,2) = 3 \), so these two values are equal, not different.
Commutativity is checked directly by comparing \( a*b \) with \( b*a \); it does not depend on associativity.
Whether an identity element exists is a separate question from commutativity; here an identity does exist, and commutativity holds regardless.

questions.question: Let \( A = \{1,2,3\} \) and \( a * b = \max(a,b) \). Which element \( e \in A \) acts as the identity for \( * \)?
options: No identity element exists in \( A \)
questions.explanation:
We need \( a * e = e * a = a \) for every \( a \in A \).

With \( e = 1 \): \( \max(1,1)=1,\ \max(2,1)=2,\ \max(3,1)=3 \), and since \( * \) is commutative this also confirms \( e * a = a \). So \( e = 1 \) is the identity.
questions.hint: Test each candidate \( e \) against every element of \( A \), on both sides.
distractor_logic: Checking \( 3 * 2 = \max(3,2) = 3 \) is fine, but \( 1 * 2 = \max(1,2) = 2 \neq 1 \), so \( 2 \) fails to leave \( 1 \) unchanged and cannot be the identity.
Checking \( 1 * 3 = \max(1,3) = 3 \neq 1 \), so \( 3 \) does not leave \( 1 \) unchanged and cannot be the identity.
The element \( 1 \) does work: \( a * 1 = \max(a,1) = a \) for every \( a \in \{1,2,3\} \), so an identity does exist.

questions.question: Let \( A = \{1,2,3\} \) and define \( a * b = a \) (the result is always the first element). Is \( * \) commutative on \( A \)?
options: No, because \( 1 * 2 = 1 \) while \( 2 * 1 = 2 \), which are not equal
Yes, because \( a * b \) always produces a valid element of \( A \)
Yes, because \( a * a = a \) for every \( a \)
Cannot be determined without a full table
questions.explanation:
Using \( a*b=a \): \( 1*2 = 1 \), but \( 2*1 = 2 \).

Since \( 1 * 2 \neq 2 * 1 \), \( * \) is not commutative on \( A \).
questions.hint: Test just one mismatched pair; a single failure is enough to rule out commutativity.
distractor_logic: Landing inside \( A \) is the closure property, not commutativity; commutativity specifically requires \( a*b=b*a \), which fails here.
That an element combined with itself returns itself is a separate fact and does not establish commutativity for mixed pairs like \( 1 \) and \( 2 \).
The rule \( a*b=a \) already lets \( 1*2 \) and \( 2*1 \) be computed directly, and they disagree, so commutativity can be ruled out without a table.

questions.question: Let \( A = \{1,2,3\} \) and \( a * b = a \). Does \( e = 1 \) act as a two-sided identity, satisfying \( a * e = e * a = a \) for every \( a \in A \)?
options: Yes, since \( a * 1 = a \) holds for every \( a \in A \)
No — \( a * 1 = a \) holds for every \( a \), but \( 1 * a = 1 \), which fails to equal \( a \) whenever \( a \neq 1 \)
Yes, since \( 1 * a = 1 \) matches the definition of \( * \)
Yes, because every operation of this form automatically has an identity
questions.explanation:
On the right: \( a * 1 = a \) for every \( a \in A \), since \( * \) always returns the first argument.

On the left: \( 1 * a = 1 \), which only equals \( a \) when \( a = 1 \). Since the left side fails for \( a=2,3 \), \( e=1 \) is only a one-sided (right) identity, not a true two-sided identity.
questions.hint: Check the identity condition on both sides separately — right-side success does not guarantee left-side success.
distractor_logic: This only checks one side of the identity condition; the other side, \( 1 * a \), must also equal \( a \), and it does not.
Matching the operation's own rule is not the same as satisfying the identity condition \( 1 * a = a \); here \( 1*a=1 \neq a \) for \( a \neq 1 \).
There is no such automatic guarantee; here checking both sides explicitly shows the identity condition genuinely fails on the left.

questions.question: Under a binary operation \( * \) on \( A \) with identity \( e \), how is the inverse of an element \( a \in A \) defined?
options: \( a^{-1} \) is an element satisfying \( a * a^{-1} = a \)
\( a^{-1} \) is simply \( \dfrac{1}{a} \) whenever \( a \neq 0 \)
\( a^{-1} \) is an element of \( A \) satisfying \( a * a^{-1} = a^{-1} * a = e \)
\( a^{-1} \) is any element of \( A \) other than \( a \)
questions.explanation:
By definition, \( a^{-1} \) is the element for which both \( a * a^{-1} = e \) and \( a^{-1} * a = e \) hold, where \( e \) is the identity of \( * \).

This mirrors the identity condition, checked on both sides.
questions.hint: The inverse must combine with \( a \), on both sides, to produce the identity \( e \) — not just any element.
distractor_logic: This wrongly equates the result with \( a \) itself rather than with the identity element \( e \).
The inverse under an abstract operation \( * \) need not be the arithmetic reciprocal; it depends entirely on how \( * \) is defined.
Being merely different from \( a \) is not sufficient; the defining condition specifically requires the combination with \( a \) to produce the identity \( e \) on both sides.

questions.question: Let \( A = \{1,2,3\} \), \( a * b = \max(a,b) \), with identity \( e = 1 \). Does \( 3 \) have an inverse under \( * \)?
options: Yes, \( 3^{-1} = 1 \), since \( 1 \) is the identity element
No — there is no \( x \in A \) with \( \max(3,x) = 1 \), since \( \max(3,x) \geq 3 \) for every \( x \in A \)
questions.explanation:
We need \( x \in A \) with \( \max(3,x) = 1 \).

But \( \max(3,x) \geq 3 \) for every \( x \in \{1,2,3\} \), so it can never equal \( 1 \). Hence \( 3 \) has no inverse under \( * \) — not every element of a binary operation needs to have one.
questions.hint: Look for \( x \) with \( 3 * x \) equal to the identity \( 1 \); check whether that is even possible.
distractor_logic: Being the identity element does not automatically make \( 1 \) the inverse of \( 3 \); checking \( \max(3,1) = 3 \neq 1 \) shows this fails.
The result \( \max(3,3) = 3 \) equals \( 3 \), not the identity \( 1 \), so this does not satisfy the inverse condition.
\( \dfrac{1}{3} \) is not even an element of \( A = \{1,2,3\} \), and the arithmetic reciprocal is irrelevant to the max operation.

questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: On the set \( \mathbb{Z} \), define \( R \) by \( (a,b) \in R \) if and only if \( a - b \) is even. Is \( R \) reflexive on \( \mathbb{Z} \)?
options: Yes, because \( a - a = 0 \) for every \( a \in \mathbb{Z} \), and \( 0 \) is even
No, because \( a - a = 0 \), and \( 0 \) is neither even nor odd
No, because evenness of \( a-b \) depends on the specific value of \( a \)
Cannot be determined without knowing whether \( a \) is positive or negative
questions.explanation:
For any \( a \in \mathbb{Z} \), \( a - a = 0 \).

Since \( 0 \) is even, \( (a,a) \in R \) for every \( a \in \mathbb{Z} \), so \( R \) is reflexive.
questions.hint: Substitute \( b = a \) into the condition and check whether the result is always even.
distractor_logic: \( 0 \) is in fact classified as an even integer, since \( 0 = 2 \times 0 \); it is not excluded from evenness.
The condition \( a - a = 0 \) is even for every choice of \( a \in \mathbb{Z} \) with no exceptions, so reflexivity holds regardless of which \( a \) is picked.
Whether \( a \) is positive, negative, or zero, \( a - a \) is always exactly \( 0 \), which is even; the sign of \( a \) is irrelevant here.

questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: On the set \( \mathbb{N} \), define \( R \) by \( (a,b) \in R \) if and only if \( a \leq b \). Is \( R \) symmetric on \( \mathbb{N} \)?
options: Yes, because \( \leq \) is a valid order on \( \mathbb{N} \)
No — for example, \( 2 \leq 3 \) so \( (2,3) \in R \), but \( 3 \leq 2 \) is false, so \( (3,2) \notin R \)
Yes, because \( a \leq a \) holds for every \( a \)
Cannot be determined without restricting \( \mathbb{N} \) to a finite subset
questions.explanation:
Take \( a = 2, b = 3 \): since \( 2 \leq 3 \), \( (2,3) \in R \).

But \( 3 \leq 2 \) is false, so \( (3,2) \notin R \). This single counterexample shows \( R \) is not symmetric.
questions.hint: Find one pair where reversing the inequality fails.
distractor_logic: Being a valid order relation does not make it symmetric; in fact the ordering \( \leq \) is precisely what breaks symmetry whenever \( a \neq b \).
That fact only confirms reflexivity; symmetry requires checking pairs with \( a \neq b \), where \( \leq \) fails to reverse.
A single counterexample, such as \( a=2, b=3 \), is already enough to disprove symmetry on the full set \( \mathbb{N} \); no restriction is needed.

questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: On the set of positive integers, define \( R \) by \( (a,b) \in R \) if and only if \( a \) divides \( b \). Is \( R \) reflexive?
options: No, because \( 1 \) divides every positive integer, not just itself
No, because division is not always defined between two positive integers
Yes, because every positive integer \( a \) divides itself, since \( a = 1 \times a \)
Cannot be determined without knowing whether \( a \) is prime
questions.explanation:
For any positive integer \( a \), we can write \( a = 1 \times a \), so \( a \) divides \( a \).

Since this holds for every positive integer, \( R \) is reflexive.
questions.hint: Check whether \( a = k \cdot a \) for some positive integer \( k \), for every \( a \).
distractor_logic: That \( 1 \) divides everything is a separate fact about the number \( 1 \); it does not affect whether every \( a \) divides itself.
Divisibility, \( a \mid a \), only requires that \( a = ka \) for some positive integer \( k \) (here \( k=1 \)); it is always well defined for positive integers.
Whether \( a \) is prime or composite, \( a = 1 \times a \) always holds, so \( a \mid a \) regardless of primality.

questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: On the set of positive integers, define \( R \) by \( (a,b) \in R \) if and only if \( a \) divides \( b \). Is \( R \) symmetric?
options: Yes, because divisibility is a natural, well-defined relation
Yes, because every number divides itself
Cannot be determined without listing every pair of positive integers
No — for example, \( 2 \) divides \( 4 \), so \( (2,4) \in R \), but \( 4 \) does not divide \( 2 \), so \( (4,2) \notin R \)
questions.explanation:
Take \( a = 2, b = 4 \): \( 2 \) divides \( 4 \), so \( (2,4) \in R \).

But \( 4 \) does not divide \( 2 \), so \( (4,2) \notin R \). Hence \( R \) is not symmetric.
questions.hint: Look for a pair \( a, b \) where \( a \) divides \( b \) but \( b \) does not divide \( a \).
distractor_logic: Being well defined does not make a relation symmetric; divisibility specifically breaks symmetry whenever \( a \neq b \).
That fact establishes reflexivity, not symmetry; symmetry concerns pairs of distinct numbers, where divisibility can fail to reverse.
A single counterexample, such as \( 2 \) and \( 4 \), is already sufficient to disprove symmetry; an exhaustive list is not required.

questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: On the set \( \mathbb{Z} \), define \( R \) by \( (a,b) \in R \) if and only if \( |a-b| \leq 1 \). Is \( R \) transitive on \( \mathbb{Z} \)?
options: No — for example, \( (1,2) \in R \) and \( (2,3) \in R \), since both differences have absolute value \( 1 \), but \( |1-3| = 2 > 1 \), so \( (1,3) \notin R \)
Yes, because \( |a-b| \leq 1 \) is a symmetric-looking condition
Yes, because \( R \) is reflexive and symmetric, so it must also be transitive
Cannot be determined without checking every triple in \( \mathbb{Z} \)
questions.explanation:
Consider \( 1, 2, 3 \): \( |1-2|=1 \) and \( |2-3|=1 \), so \( (1,2), (2,3) \in R \).

But \( |1-3| = 2 \), which exceeds \( 1 \), so \( (1,3) \notin R \). This chain breaks transitivity.
questions.hint: Try a short chain of consecutive integers and see whether the endpoints stay within distance \( 1 \).
distractor_logic: Symmetric-looking is not the same as transitive; the chain \( 1,2,3 \) is a direct counterexample showing transitivity fails.
Reflexivity and symmetry never guarantee transitivity; they are independent properties, and here transitivity genuinely fails.
A single counterexample, such as the chain \( 1,2,3 \), is already enough to disprove transitivity for the whole set.

questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: On the set \( \mathbb{Z} \), define \( R \) by \( (a,b) \in R \) if and only if \( a + b \) is even. Is \( R \) symmetric on \( \mathbb{Z} \)?
options: No, because addition does not always produce an even result
Yes, because \( a + b = b + a \), so if \( a+b \) is even then \( b+a \) is automatically the same even number
No, because the condition depends on the order in which \( a \) and \( b \) are added
Cannot be determined without knowing the sign of \( a \) and \( b \)
questions.explanation:
Since \( a + b = b + a \) always holds for integers, whenever \( (a,b) \in R \) (i.e. \( a+b \) is even), the same sum shows \( (b,a) \in R \) too.

So \( R \) is symmetric on \( \mathbb{Z} \).
questions.hint: Recall that ordinary addition of integers is commutative.
distractor_logic: Whether \( a+b \) itself is even or odd is irrelevant to symmetry; what matters is that whenever it is even, reversing the order gives the identical sum.
Ordinary addition is commutative, so \( a+b \) and \( b+a \) are always exactly the same number, meaning order cannot matter here.
Since addition is commutative for all integers regardless of sign, the symmetry argument holds unconditionally.

questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: On the set \( \mathbb{Z} \), define \( R \) by \( (a,b) \in R \) if and only if \( a - b \) is a multiple of \( 3 \). Is \( R \) transitive on \( \mathbb{Z} \)?
options: No, because \( a - c \) is generally larger than \( a - b \) or \( b - c \)
No, because multiples of \( 3 \) are not closed under addition
Yes — if \( a-b = 3k \) and \( b-c = 3m \) for integers \( k, m \), then \( a - c = 3(k+m) \), which is also a multiple of \( 3 \)
Cannot be determined without specific numerical values for \( a, b, c \)
questions.explanation:
Given \( a-b=3k \) and \( b-c=3m \), adding gives \( a-c = (a-b)+(b-c) = 3k+3m = 3(k+m) \).

Since \( k+m \) is an integer, \( a-c \) is a multiple of \( 3 \), so \( (a,c) \in R \). Hence \( R \) is transitive.
questions.hint: Write \( a-c \) as the sum \( (a-b)+(b-c) \) and use closure of multiples of \( 3 \) under addition.
distractor_logic: The size of \( a-c \) is irrelevant; what matters is whether it remains a multiple of \( 3 \), and the algebra confirms that it always does.
Multiples of \( 3 \) are in fact closed under addition: adding \( 3k \) and \( 3m \) gives \( 3(k+m) \), still a multiple of \( 3 \).
The algebraic identity \( a-c=(a-b)+(b-c) \) proves transitivity for all integers at once, with no need for specific numbers.

questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: On the set \( \mathbb{N} \), define \( R \) by \( (a,b) \in R \) if and only if \( a > b \). Is \( R \) reflexive on \( \mathbb{N} \)?
options: Yes, because every natural number is greater than some other number
Yes, because \( \mathbb{N} \) contains infinitely many elements
Cannot be determined without knowing if \( 0 \in \mathbb{N} \) in this context
No, because \( a > a \) is false for every \( a \in \mathbb{N} \)
questions.explanation:
For any \( a \in \mathbb{N} \), the statement \( a > a \) is never true, since a number cannot be strictly greater than itself.

Since \( (a,a) \notin R \) for every \( a \), \( R \) is not reflexive.
questions.hint: Substitute \( b=a \) into the strict inequality and check whether it can ever be true.
distractor_logic: Reflexivity specifically requires \( a > a \) for the same element \( a \), not merely \( a \) being greater than some other, different number.
The size of \( \mathbb{N} \) has no bearing on reflexivity; the condition \( a>a \) is false for every single \( a \), regardless of how many elements exist.
Whether or not \( 0 \) is included, the statement \( a>a \) is false for that value just as it is for every other natural number.

questions.question: On \( \mathbb{Z} \), define \( R \) by \( (a,b) \in R \) if and only if \( a-b \) is even. Why is \( R \) an equivalence relation on \( \mathbb{Z} \)?
options: Because \( a-a=0 \) is even (reflexive), \( a-b \) even implies \( b-a \) even (symmetric), and evenness is preserved under addition of the two differences (transitive)
Because every pair \( (a,b) \) satisfies \( a-b \) is even
Because \( R \) is reflexive; reflexivity alone is enough to guarantee an equivalence relation
Because \( \mathbb{Z} \) is an infinite set, and every relation on an infinite set is automatically an equivalence relation
questions.explanation:
Reflexive: \( a-a=0 \) is even for every \( a \).

Symmetric: if \( a-b \) is even then \( b-a=-(a-b) \) is also even.

Transitive: if \( a-b \) and \( b-c \) are both even, their sum \( a-c=(a-b)+(b-c) \) is even too. All three hold, so \( R \) is an equivalence relation.
questions.hint: All three properties — reflexive, symmetric, transitive — must be verified from the condition itself.
distractor_logic: This is false in general — for example \( a=1, b=2 \) gives \( a-b=-1 \), which is odd, so not every pair satisfies the condition.
Reflexivity alone is not sufficient; symmetry and transitivity must also be verified independently.
The size of the underlying set has no bearing on whether a relation is an equivalence relation; each of the three properties must be checked directly.

questions.question: Continuing with \( R \) on \( \mathbb{Z} \) defined by \( a-b \) even, which set correctly describes the equivalence class \( [0] \)?
options: \( [0] = \{x \in \mathbb{Z} : x \text{ is even}\} \)
\( [0] = \{x \in \mathbb{Z} : x \text{ is odd}\} \)
questions.explanation:
By definition, \( [0] = \{x \in \mathbb{Z} : (x,0) \in R\} = \{x \in \mathbb{Z} : x - 0 \text{ is even}\} \).

Since \( x - 0 = x \), this is exactly the set of even integers.
questions.hint: An element \( x \) belongs to \( [0] \) exactly when \( x - 0 \) is even.
distractor_logic: This misses every other even integer, such as \( 2 \) and \( -4 \), which also satisfy \( x - 0 \) even.
An odd \( x \) gives \( x - 0 = x \), which is odd, not even, so odd integers do not belong to \( [0] \).
This wrongly includes odd integers as well; only even integers satisfy \( x-0 \) is even.

questions.question: On \( \mathbb{Z} \), define \( R \) by \( (a,b) \in R \) if and only if \( a - b \) is a multiple of \( 5 \) (i.e. \( a \equiv b \pmod 5 \)). Is \( R \) an equivalence relation on \( \mathbb{Z} \)?
options: No, because \( 5 \) does not divide every integer
No, because congruence relations are only symmetric, not transitive
Yes, since congruence modulo \( 5 \) is reflexive (\( a-a=0 \)), symmetric (\( a-b \) a multiple of 5 implies \( b-a \) is too), and transitive (multiples of 5 add to a multiple of 5)
Cannot be determined without listing all pairs \( (a,b) \)
questions.explanation:
Reflexive: \( a-a=0 \), a multiple of \( 5 \).

Symmetric: if \( a-b=5k \), then \( b-a=-5k \), also a multiple of \( 5 \).

Transitive: if \( a-b=5k \) and \( b-c=5m \), then \( a-c=5(k+m) \). All three hold, so \( R \) is an equivalence relation.
questions.hint: Congruence modulo a fixed number is a standard equivalence relation; verify each property with the divisibility condition.
distractor_logic: The relation never requires \( 5 \) to divide every integer directly; it requires \( 5 \) to divide the difference \( a-b \), which is a much weaker and always well-defined condition.
Congruence modulo any fixed integer is transitive as well; the sum of two multiples of \( 5 \) is again a multiple of \( 5 \).
The three properties follow from a short general algebraic argument on \( a-b \), valid for every integer, so an exhaustive list is unnecessary.

questions.question: Using the congruence-modulo-5 relation from above, which set correctly describes \( [2] \)?
options: \( [2] = \{x \in \mathbb{Z} : x \text{ is a multiple of } 2\} \)
\( [2] = \{x \in \mathbb{Z} : x \text{ is a multiple of } 5\} \)
\( [2] = \{x \in \mathbb{Z} : x - 2 \text{ is a multiple of } 5\} \)
questions.explanation:
By definition, \( [2] = \{x \in \mathbb{Z} : (x,2) \in R\} = \{x \in \mathbb{Z} : x-2 \text{ is a multiple of } 5\} \).

This includes \( \ldots, -8, -3, 2, 7, 12, \ldots \), every integer congruent to \( 2 \) modulo \( 5 \).
questions.hint: An element \( x \) belongs to \( [2] \) exactly when \( x - 2 \) is a multiple of \( 5 \).
distractor_logic: This misses every other integer congruent to \( 2 \pmod 5 \), such as \( 7, -3, 12 \), which also satisfy the condition.
This describes even integers, which is unrelated to being congruent to \( 2 \) modulo \( 5 \).
This describes \( [0] \), the class of integers congruent to \( 0 \) modulo \( 5 \), not \( [2] \).

questions.question: On the set \( \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\} \), define \( R \) by \( (a,b) \in R \) if and only if \( ab > 0 \). Is \( R \) an equivalence relation?
options: Yes — it is reflexive since \( a \cdot a = a^2 > 0 \), symmetric since \( ab = ba \), and transitive since \( a,b \) sharing a sign and \( b,c \) sharing a sign forces \( a,c \) to share a sign too
No, because \( ab > 0 \) fails whenever \( a \) or \( b \) is negative
No, because \( 0 \) has been excluded from the domain, making reflexivity impossible
Yes, but only symmetric and transitive, not reflexive
questions.explanation:
Reflexive: \( a \cdot a = a^2 > 0 \) since \( a \neq 0 \).

Symmetric: \( ab = ba \), so the sign of the product is unaffected by order.

Transitive: if \( a,b \) share a sign and \( b,c \) share a sign, then \( a,c \) must also share that sign, so \( ac>0 \). All three hold.
questions.hint: Think of \( ab>0 \) as saying \( a \) and \( b \) share the same sign, and check that sharing a sign behaves transitively.
distractor_logic: The condition \( ab>0 \) is satisfied precisely when \( a \) and \( b \) share the same sign, including when both are negative; it does not fail there.
Excluding \( 0 \) is exactly what preserves reflexivity, since \( a^2>0 \) requires \( a \neq 0 \); reflexivity holds for every remaining element.
Reflexivity does hold, since \( a \cdot a = a^2 \), and \( a^2 > 0 \) for every nonzero real \( a \).

questions.question: For the equivalence relation \( (a,b) \in R \iff ab>0 \) on \( \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\} \), how many distinct equivalence classes does \( R \) create?
options: \( 2 \) — the set of positive reals and the set of negative reals
Infinitely many, one for each real number
\( 3 \) — positive reals, negative reals, and \( \{0\} \)
questions.explanation:
Every pair of positive reals satisfies \( ab>0 \), so all positives fall into one class; similarly all negatives fall into another class.

A positive and a negative never satisfy \( ab>0 \), so the two classes are distinct. This gives exactly \( 2 \) equivalence classes.
questions.hint: Group numbers by sign, since \( ab>0 \) exactly means \( a \) and \( b \) share a sign.
distractor_logic: A single class would require every nonzero real to be related to every other; but a positive number and a negative number never satisfy \( ab>0 \), so they cannot share a class.
Any two positive reals are always related, since their product is positive, so they collapse into one shared class rather than each forming its own.
\( 0 \) has already been excluded from the domain \( \mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\} \), so it cannot form a class of its own here.

questions.question: On \( \mathbb{R} \), define \( R \) by \( (a,b) \in R \) if and only if \( a - b \in \mathbb{Z} \) (their difference is an integer). Is \( R \) an equivalence relation on \( \mathbb{R} \)?
options: No, because most real numbers are not integers themselves
No, because \( \mathbb{Z} \) is not closed under subtraction of real numbers
Yes — \( a-a=0 \in \mathbb{Z} \) (reflexive), \( a-b \in \mathbb{Z} \implies b-a \in \mathbb{Z} \) (symmetric), and the sum of two integers is an integer (transitive)
Cannot be determined without restricting \( \mathbb{R} \) to rational numbers
questions.explanation:
Reflexive: \( a-a=0 \in \mathbb{Z} \).

Symmetric: if \( a-b=n \in \mathbb{Z} \), then \( b-a=-n \in \mathbb{Z} \).

Transitive: if \( a-b=n \) and \( b-c=m \) with \( n,m \in \mathbb{Z} \), then \( a-c=n+m \in \mathbb{Z} \). All three hold, so \( R \) is an equivalence relation.
questions.hint: Use the fact that integers are closed under negation and addition.
distractor_logic: Whether \( a \) or \( b \) individually is an integer is irrelevant; only their difference \( a-b \) needs to be an integer, which can happen for many non-integer reals, such as \( a=2.5, b=1.5 \).
\( \mathbb{Z} \) is in fact closed under both addition and subtraction of integers; the relevant closure property here — sums of integers stay integers — is what makes transitivity work.
The argument for reflexive, symmetric and transitive works directly with real numbers and never requires restricting to rationals.

questions.question: On the set \( A = \{1,2,3,\ldots,9\} \), define \( R \) by \( (a,b) \in R \) if and only if \( a \) and \( b \) leave the same remainder when divided by \( 3 \). How many distinct equivalence classes does \( R \) create on \( A \)?
options: \( 9 \), one class per element
\( 1 \), since \( R \) is an equivalence relation and every equivalence relation has exactly one class
\( 2 \), one for odd remainders and one for even remainders
\( 3 \) — corresponding to remainders \( 0, 1, 2 \)
questions.explanation:
Remainder \( 0 \): \( \{3,6,9\} \). Remainder \( 1 \): \( \{1,4,7\} \). Remainder \( 2 \): \( \{2,5,8\} \).

These three groups partition \( A \) completely, giving exactly \( 3 \) equivalence classes.
questions.hint: List the possible remainders when dividing by \( 3 \), and group the numbers \( 1 \) to \( 9 \) by remainder.
distractor_logic: Numbers sharing the same remainder are grouped together, such as \( 3,6,9 \) all leaving remainder \( 0 \); they do not each form a separate class.
An equivalence relation can and typically does produce several classes; here the possible remainders \( 0,1,2 \) split \( A \) into three groups.
Remainders modulo \( 3 \) are \( 0, 1, 2 \), not simply odd or even; each distinct remainder value gives its own class, yielding three, not two.

questions.question: Let \( f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \) be given by \( f(x) = 2x+3 \). Is \( f \) one-one?
options: Yes — if \( f(x_1)=f(x_2) \), then \( 2x_1+3=2x_2+3 \), which forces \( x_1=x_2 \)
No, because a linear function can never be one-one
No, because the graph of \( f \) is a straight line, and straight lines repeat values
Cannot be determined without restricting the domain further
questions.explanation:
Assume \( f(x_1) = f(x_2) \), i.e. \( 2x_1+3 = 2x_2+3 \).

Subtracting \( 3 \) and dividing by \( 2 \) gives \( x_1 = x_2 \). So \( f \) is one-one.
questions.hint: Set \( f(x_1)=f(x_2) \) and solve to see whether \( x_1 \) must equal \( x_2 \).
distractor_logic: Linear functions with a nonzero slope, like this one, are in fact always one-one; only a constant function (slope zero) fails to be injective.
A non-horizontal straight line never repeats a \( y \)-value for two different \( x \)-values; repetition would only occur for a horizontal line.
The algebraic argument \( f(x_1)=f(x_2) \implies x_1=x_2 \) already works for the full domain \( \mathbb{R} \), so no restriction is needed.

questions.question: Let \( f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \) be given by \( f(x) = 2x+3 \). Is \( f \) onto?
options: No, because \( f(x) \) is always positive
Yes — for any \( y \in \mathbb{R} \), choosing \( x = \dfrac{y-3}{2} \) gives \( f(x) = y \)
No, because \( f \) is already one-one, and a function cannot be both one-one and onto
Cannot be determined without restricting the codomain to positive reals
questions.explanation:
Given any \( y \in \mathbb{R} \), solve \( 2x+3=y \) to get \( x = \dfrac{y-3}{2} \), which is a real number.

Substituting back, \( f\left(\dfrac{y-3}{2}\right) = y \), so every \( y \) has a pre-image. Hence \( f \) is onto.
questions.hint: For an arbitrary target value \( y \), try to solve \( 2x+3=y \) for \( x \).
distractor_logic: \( f(x)=2x+3 \) can take any real value, including negative ones, by choosing \( x \) sufficiently negative; it is not restricted to positive outputs.
One-one and onto are independent properties that can both hold simultaneously; here \( f \) is in fact both, making it bijective.
The codomain is already stated as all of \( \mathbb{R} \); the pre-image formula \( x=(y-3)/2 \) works for every real \( y \) without any restriction.

questions.question: Let \( f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \) be given by \( f(x) = x^2 \). Is \( f \) one-one?
options: Yes, because \( x^2 \) always produces a non-negative result
Yes, because \( f(x_1)=f(x_2) \) forces \( x_1=x_2 \) after taking square roots
No — for example, \( f(1) = 1 \) and \( f(-1) = 1 \), so two distinct inputs give the same output
Cannot be determined without knowing the sign of \( x \)
questions.explanation:
Take \( x_1 = 1 \) and \( x_2 = -1 \): both give \( f(x_1) = f(x_2) = 1 \), yet \( x_1 \neq x_2 \).

This single counterexample shows \( f \) is not one-one on \( \mathbb{R} \).
questions.hint: Try a positive value and its negative — do they give the same output?
distractor_logic: Producing only non-negative outputs concerns the range, not injectivity; the actual problem is that \( x \) and \( -x \) always give the same output.
Taking a square root only recovers \( |x_1|=|x_2| \), which allows \( x_1=-x_2 \) as well; it does not force \( x_1=x_2 \) uniquely.
The counterexample \( x=1 \) and \( x=-1 \) already settles the question directly, without needing any further assumption about sign.

questions.question: Let \( f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \) be given by \( f(x) = x^2 \). Is \( f \) onto?
options: Yes, because every real number can be squared
Yes, because \( x^2 \geq 0 \) covers all of \( \mathbb{R} \)
Cannot be determined without restricting the domain to positive numbers
No — for example, \( y = -1 \) has no real pre-image, since \( x^2 = -1 \) has no solution in \( \mathbb{R} \)
questions.explanation:
Since \( x^2 \geq 0 \) for every real \( x \), no negative number can ever be an output.

For instance, \( y=-1 \) has no real \( x \) with \( x^2=-1 \). So \( f \) is not onto \( \mathbb{R} \).
questions.hint: Check whether every real number, including negative ones, can appear as \( x^2 \).
distractor_logic: That every real number can be squared only shows every input produces an output; it says nothing about whether negative targets like \( -1 \) are ever produced.
The condition \( x^2 \geq 0 \) shows the outputs are confined to non-negative reals only, which is exactly why negative targets such as \( -1 \) are missed.
The codomain here is stated as the full \( \mathbb{R} \); regardless of any domain restriction, negative numbers like \( -1 \) can never appear as an output of \( x^2 \).

questions.question: Let \( f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \) be given by \( f(x) = x^2 \). Is \( f \) one-one?
options: Yes — since \( \mathbb{N} \) contains only non-negative values, \( f(x_1)=f(x_2) \) forces \( x_1=x_2 \) with no negative counterexample available
No, for the same reason it failed on \( \mathbb{R} \): \( f(1)=f(-1) \)
No, because squaring is never one-one on any domain
Cannot be determined without also checking whether \( f \) is onto \( \mathbb{N} \)
questions.explanation:
On \( \mathbb{N} \), every element is non-negative, so if \( x_1^2 = x_2^2 \) with \( x_1,x_2 \in \mathbb{N} \), taking the non-negative square root gives \( x_1=x_2 \).

The earlier problem (\( 1 \) and \( -1 \)) cannot occur here since \( -1 \notin \mathbb{N} \). So restricting the domain makes \( f \) one-one.
questions.hint: Ask whether the earlier counterexample for one-one-ness on \( \mathbb{R} \) is even available inside \( \mathbb{N} \).
distractor_logic: The counterexample \( x=-1 \) is not available here, since \( -1 \notin \mathbb{N} \); restricting the domain to \( \mathbb{N} \) removes this problem entirely.
Squaring fails to be one-one only when a domain contains both a number and its negative; on \( \mathbb{N} \), where every element is non-negative, this issue disappears.
One-one-ness is checked directly from the injectivity condition; it does not depend on first resolving whether \( f \) is onto.

questions.question: Let \( f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \) be given by \( f(x) = x^3 \). Is \( f \) bijective?
options: No, it is one-one but not onto, since negative numbers have no cube root
Yes — it is one-one since \( x_1^3=x_2^3 \implies x_1=x_2 \) for reals, and onto since every real \( y \) has a real cube root \( y^{1/3} \)
No, it is onto but not one-one, since \( f(1)=f(-1) \) just like \( x^2 \)
No, because odd-degree functions can never be bijective on \( \mathbb{R} \)
questions.explanation:
One-one: if \( x_1^3 = x_2^3 \), taking cube roots (unique for reals, unlike square roots) gives \( x_1=x_2 \).

Onto: for any \( y \in \mathbb{R} \), \( x=y^{1/3} \) is a real number with \( f(x)=y \). Both hold, so \( f \) is bijective.
questions.hint: Unlike squaring, cubing preserves sign, so try the same style of check used for \( x^2 \) and see if it still breaks.
distractor_logic: Every real number, including negative ones, has a real cube root — for example \( (-8)^{1/3}=-2 \) — so onto-ness does not fail here.
Unlike squaring, cubing does not repeat values: \( 1^3=1 \) while \( (-1)^3=-1 \), so these two inputs give different outputs.
Odd-degree functions such as \( x^3 \) (with positive leading behavior) are in fact classic examples of bijections on \( \mathbb{R} \), unlike even-degree functions.

questions.question: Let \( f : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z} \) be given by \( f(x) = 2x \). Is \( f \) onto?
options: Yes, because \( f \) is one-one, and every one-one function on \( \mathbb{Z} \) is also onto
Yes, because doubling any integer still gives an integer
No — for example, \( y = 3 \) has no pre-image, since \( 2x=3 \) has no solution with \( x \in \mathbb{Z} \)
Cannot be determined without restricting the codomain to even integers
questions.explanation:
The image of \( f \) is exactly the set of even integers, since \( f(x)=2x \) is always even.

Since \( 3 \) is odd, no \( x \in \mathbb{Z} \) satisfies \( 2x=3 \). So \( f \) is not onto \( \mathbb{Z} \).
questions.hint: Try to hit an odd target value and see whether an integer solution exists.
distractor_logic: One-one-ness never guarantees onto-ness; here \( f \) is one-one yet fails to be onto because odd integers like \( 3 \) are never produced.
That the output always lands back in \( \mathbb{Z} \) is the closure/well-defined property of \( f \); it does not mean every integer, including odd ones, is actually produced as an output.
The codomain is explicitly stated as all of \( \mathbb{Z} \); under that codomain, the odd integer \( 3 \) is a valid, ready counterexample with no restriction needed.

questions.question: Let \( f : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{N} \cup \{0\} \) be given by \( f(x) = |x| \). Is \( f \) one-one?
options: Yes, because \( |x| \) is always non-negative
Yes, because absolute value is a well-defined function
Cannot be determined without knowing whether \( x \) is even or odd
No — for example, \( f(1) = 1 \) and \( f(-1) = 1 \), so two distinct integers share the same image
questions.explanation:
For \( x=1 \) and \( x=-1 \), both give \( |x|=1 \), yet \( 1 \neq -1 \).

This shows two distinct elements of \( \mathbb{Z} \) share the same image, so \( f \) is not one-one.
questions.hint: Compare the images of a number and its negative.
distractor_logic: Always being non-negative describes the range of \( f \); it says nothing about whether two different inputs can share an output, which is what one-one-ness requires.
Being well-defined only guarantees each input has exactly one output; it does not prevent two different inputs, like \( 1 \) and \( -1 \), from sharing that output.
The parity of \( x \) is irrelevant here; any nonzero integer and its negative already give a direct counterexample regardless of whether they are even or odd.

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: Let \( f, g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \) be given by \( f(x) = 2x+3 \) and \( g(x) = x-1 \). Find \( (g \circ f)(x) \).
questions.hint: Substitute \( f(x) \) into \( g \): compute \( g(f(x)) \).
distractor_logic: This is \( f(x) \) itself, without applying \( g \) to it afterward.
This is actually the value of \( (f \circ g)(x) \), the composition in the reverse order.
This subtracts \( 1 \) twice instead of once — a common slip when substituting \( g(x)=x-1 \) into \( f \) rather than the other way around.

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: Using the same \( f(x)=2x+3 \) and \( g(x)=x-1 \) on \( \mathbb{R} \), find \( (f \circ g)(x) \).
questions.explanation:
\( (f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x)) = f(x-1) \).

Now apply \( f \): \( f(x-1) = 2(x-1)+3 = 2x-2+3 = 2x+1 \). Note this differs from \( (g\circ f)(x) = 2x+2 \) found earlier, confirming order matters.
questions.hint: Substitute \( g(x) \) into \( f \): compute \( f(g(x)) \).
distractor_logic: This is the value of \( (g \circ f)(x) \), found by applying \( f \) first instead of \( g \) first.
This is \( g(x) \) itself, without then applying \( f \) to that result.
This comes from adding \( 1 \) instead of subtracting it inside \( f \), reversing the sign of the constant from \( g \).

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: Let \( f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \) be given by \( f(x) = 2x+3 \). Since \( f \) is bijective, find \( f^{-1}(x) \).
questions.explanation:
Let \( y = 2x+3 \).

Solving for \( x \): \( x = \dfrac{y-3}{2} \). Renaming \( y \) as \( x \) gives \( f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x-3}{2} \).
questions.hint: Set \( y=f(x) \), solve for \( x \) in terms of \( y \), then rename \( y \) as \( x \).
distractor_logic: This is the reciprocal \( \dfrac{1}{f(x)} \), not the inverse function; \( f^{-1} \) must undo \( f \), not divide by its value.
This does not undo \( f \) correctly: substituting back, \( f(2x-3) = 2(2x-3)+3 = 4x-3 \neq x \) in general.
The sign on the constant term is wrong; it should be subtracted, not added, when solving \( y=2x+3 \) for \( x \).

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: Let \( f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \) be given by \( f(x) = 3x-5 \). Find \( f^{-1}(x) \).
questions.explanation:
Let \( y = 3x-5 \).

Adding \( 5 \): \( y+5 = 3x \). Dividing by \( 3 \): \( x = \dfrac{y+5}{3} \). Renaming \( y \) as \( x \) gives \( f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x+5}{3} \).
questions.hint: Set \( y=3x-5 \) and isolate \( x \).
distractor_logic: The sign on the constant is wrong; solving \( y=3x-5 \) for \( x \) requires adding \( 5 \), not subtracting it.
This does not correctly reverse the operations of \( f \); it neither divides by \( 3 \) nor adds \( 5 \) in the right combination.
This is the reciprocal \( \dfrac{1}{f(x)} \), a completely different quantity from the inverse function \( f^{-1}(x) \).

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: Let \( f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \) be given by \( f(x) = x^3+2 \). Find \( f^{-1}(x) \).
questions.explanation:
Let \( y = x^3+2 \).

Subtracting \( 2 \): \( x^3 = y-2 \). Taking the cube root: \( x = (y-2)^{1/3} \). Renaming \( y \) as \( x \) gives \( f^{-1}(x) = (x-2)^{1/3} \).
questions.hint: Set \( y=x^3+2 \), isolate \( x^3 \) first, then take a cube root.
distractor_logic: This subtracts \( 2 \) after taking the cube root, but the correct steps require subtracting \( 2 \) first and only then taking the cube root.
The sign on the constant is wrong; solving \( y=x^3+2 \) for \( x \) requires subtracting \( 2 \), not adding it, before taking the cube root.
This is the reciprocal \( \dfrac{1}{f(x)} \), not the inverse function that undoes \( f \).

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: Let \( f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \) be given by \( f(x) = x+3 \). Find \( f^{-1}(x) \), and note how it differs from \( \dfrac{1}{f(x)} \).
options: \( f^{-1}(x) = x-3 \), which is entirely different from \( \dfrac{1}{f(x)} = \dfrac{1}{x+3} \)
questions.explanation:
Let \( y = x+3 \), so \( x = y-3 \), giving \( f^{-1}(x) = x-3 \).

This is a completely different expression from \( \dfrac{1}{f(x)} = \dfrac{1}{x+3} \); the two must never be confused.
questions.hint: Solve \( y=x+3 \) for \( x \) to find the true inverse, and compare it against \( 1/f(x) \) to see they are unrelated.
distractor_logic: This computes the reciprocal of \( f(x) \) rather than reversing the rule of \( f \); the true inverse is \( x-3 \).
This has the wrong sign on \( x \); solving \( y=x+3 \) for \( x \) gives \( x=y-3 \), not \( 3-y \).
This simply repeats \( f \) itself rather than reversing it; substituting back, \( f(f(x)) = x+6 \neq x \), so this is not the inverse.

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: Let \( f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \) be given by \( f(x) = 5x-7 \). Find \( f^{-1}(3) \).
questions.hint: Solve \( 5x-7=3 \) directly for \( x \) — that value of \( x \) is \( f^{-1}(3) \).
distractor_logic: This treats the question as asking for \( \dfrac{1}{f(3)} \) rather than the actual inverse-function value \( f^{-1}(3) \).
This is \( f(3) = 5(3)-7 = 8 \), the forward value of \( f \) at \( 3 \), not the inverse value \( f^{-1}(3) \).
This comes from multiplying \( 3 \) by \( 5 \) without correctly reversing both operations of \( f \).

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: Let \( f(x) = 2x+1 \) and \( g(x) = \dfrac{x-1}{2} \), both functions \( \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \). Compute \( (g \circ f)(x) \) to check whether \( g = f^{-1} \).
options: \( (g \circ f)(x) = 2x \), so \( g \neq f^{-1} \)
\( (g \circ f)(x) \) cannot confirm \( g=f^{-1} \); only \( (f \circ g)(x) \) can
\( (g \circ f)(x) = x \), confirming \( g = f^{-1} \)
questions.explanation:
\( (g \circ f)(x) = g(2x+1) = \dfrac{(2x+1)-1}{2} = \dfrac{2x}{2} = x \).

Since \( (g\circ f)(x)=x \) for every \( x \), \( g \) reverses \( f \) exactly, confirming \( g = f^{-1} \).
questions.hint: Substitute \( f(x) \) into \( g \) and simplify fully.
distractor_logic: Carrying out the substitution correctly gives exactly \( x \), not \( 2x \); a division step was skipped in this option.
Carrying out the substitution correctly, the \( +1 \) and \( -1 \) terms cancel completely, leaving just \( x \), not \( x+1 \).
For functions on the same set, checking either composition equal to the identity is valid evidence that the two functions are inverses of each other.

questions.question: On \( \mathbb{Z} \), define \( a * b = a+b-ab \). Is \( * \) commutative on \( \mathbb{Z} \)?
options: Yes, because \( a+b-ab = b+a-ba \) for every \( a, b \), since ordinary addition and multiplication are both commutative
No, because subtraction is involved, and subtraction is not commutative
No, because \( a*b \) depends on which variable is squared
Cannot be determined without trying specific numbers
questions.explanation:
Swapping gives \( b*a = b+a-ba \).

Since addition and multiplication of real numbers are commutative, \( b+a-ba = a+b-ab = a*b \). So \( * \) is commutative.
questions.hint: Swap \( a \) and \( b \) in the formula and see if the expression is unchanged.
distractor_logic: The subtraction here is of the single product term \( ab \), which is itself symmetric in \( a \) and \( b \); this does not break the overall symmetry of the expression.
No variable is squared anywhere in the expression \( a+b-ab \), so this concern does not apply.
The algebraic expression \( a+b-ab \) is symmetric in \( a \) and \( b \) by inspection, which settles commutativity for all values at once.

questions.question: On \( \mathbb{Z} \), define \( a * b = a+b-ab \). Is \( * \) associative on \( \mathbb{Z} \)?
options: No, because \( a*b*c \) is not the same as ordinary addition of three numbers
Yes — expanding both \( (a*b)*c \) and \( a*(b*c) \) gives the same expression, \( a+b+c-ab-bc-ca+abc \)
No, because the operation involves a product term \( ab \), and products are never associative when combined with sums
Cannot be determined without picking specific numerical values for \( a,b,c \)
questions.explanation:
\( (a*b)*c = (a+b-ab)+c-(a+b-ab)c = a+b+c-ab-ac-bc+abc \).

\( a*(b*c) = a+(b+c-bc)-a(b+c-bc) = a+b+c-bc-ab-ac+abc \). Both expansions match exactly, so \( * \) is associative.
questions.hint: Expand \( (a*b)*c \) and \( a*(b*c) \) fully in terms of \( a,b,c \) and compare.
