questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: On \( \mathbb{Z} \), define \( a R b \) iff \( f(a) \le f(b) \), where \( f(x)=x^2 \). Which properties does \( R \) satisfy?
options: \( R \) is reflexive and transitive, but not symmetric
\( R \) is symmetric, since \( f(a)\le f(b) \) and \( f(b)\le f(a) \) both describe the same relationship
\( R \) is an equivalence relation, since it is built from a well-defined function
\( R \) is not reflexive, since \( f(a) \le f(a) \) requires \( f \) to be strictly increasing
questions.explanation:
Reflexive: \( f(a) \le f(a) \) always holds trivially.

Transitive: \( f(a)\le f(b) \) and \( f(b)\le f(c) \) give \( f(a)\le f(c) \), since \( \le \) on real numbers is transitive.

Symmetric fails: with \( a=1,b=2 \), \( f(1)=1\le f(2)=4 \) holds, but \( f(2)=4 \le f(1)=1 \) does not.
questions.hint: Reflexivity and transitivity follow directly from the ordinary \( \le \) order; test symmetry with two specific unequal values.
distractor_logic: Checking directly with \( a=1,b=2 \): \( f(1)=1\le f(2)=4 \) holds, but \( f(2)=4\le f(1)=1 \) does not; symmetry genuinely fails.

Being built from a function does not guarantee symmetry; reflexivity and transitivity hold here because they mirror properties of the ordinary \( \le \) order, but symmetry does not follow from that order.
The non-strict inequality \( f(a)\le f(a) \) holds trivially for every \( a \), regardless of whether \( f \) is increasing, decreasing, or neither.
mixed_topics: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive

questions.question: On \( \mathbb{R} \), define \( a R b \) iff \( a^3=b^3 \). Confirm \( R \) is an equivalence relation and describe its equivalence classes.
options: Every class contains exactly two elements, \( a \) and \( -a \), just as with \( x^2 \)
\( R \) is an equivalence relation (the kernel of \( f(x)=x^3 \)), and since \( f \) is one-one on \( \mathbb{R} \), every equivalence class is a singleton: \( [a]=\{a\} \)
\( R \) is not an equivalence relation since cubes can be negative
\( [a] \) is infinite for every \( a \), since infinitely many reals have the same cube
questions.explanation:
\( R \) is the kernel relation of \( f(x)=x^3 \), so it is automatically reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

Since \( f \) is one-one on \( \mathbb{R} \) (strictly increasing), \( a^3=b^3 \) forces \( a=b \); so every equivalence class is just \( \{a\} \).
questions.hint: Recall that cubing is strictly increasing and hence one-one on all of \( \mathbb{R} \), unlike squaring.
distractor_logic: This pattern belongs to the even function \( x^2 \), not \( x^3 \); since \( (-a)^3=-a^3 \ne a^3 \) whenever \( a \ne 0 \), cubing does not pair \( a \) with \( -a \) at all.

Whether the output is negative or positive has no bearing on the defining properties of \( R \); reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity all follow purely from equality of the real numbers \( a^3 \) and \( b^3 \).
The cube function is one-one on \( \mathbb{R} \), so exactly one real number produces any given cube value; each equivalence class therefore contains only a single element.

questions.question: On \( \mathbb{R} \), define \( a*b=a+b \) (ordinary addition) and let \( f(x)=x+1 \). Does \( f(a*b)=f(a)+f(b) \) hold for every \( a,b \in \mathbb{R} \)?
options: Yes, because \( f \) is a linear function and every linear function preserves addition
Yes, because adding \( 1 \) to each side keeps both sides balanced
No — for example, with \( a=b=1 \): \( f(1*1)=f(2)=3 \), while \( f(1)+f(1)=2+2=4 \), which are not equal
Cannot be determined without knowing whether \( f \) is one-one
questions.explanation:
\( f(a*b) = f(a+b) = a+b+1 \).

\( f(a)+f(b) = (a+1)+(b+1) = a+b+2 \). These differ by \( 1 \) for every \( a,b \); for instance at \( a=b=1 \), \( f(2)=3 \) while \( f(1)+f(1)=4 \).
questions.hint: Substitute a simple pair such as \( a=b=1 \) into both sides and compare the results directly.
distractor_logic: Only linear functions with zero constant term, of the form \( f(x)=cx \), preserve addition in this sense; \( f(x)=x+1 \) carries an extra constant \( 1 \) that breaks the identity.
Adding \( 1 \) once to the sum \( a+b \) is not the same as adding \( 1 \) separately to \( a \) and to \( b \); the right-hand side picks up an extra \( 1 \) that the left-hand side does not.
Injectivity of \( f \) has no bearing on this identity; it can be checked directly by substitution regardless of whether \( f \) is one-one.
mixed_topics: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions

questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: On \( \mathbb{Z} \), define \( a R b \) iff \( |a-b| \le 2 \). Which of the three equivalence properties does \( R \) fail?
options: \( R \) fails reflexivity, since \( |a-a|=0 \) is not always less than or equal to \( 2 \)
\( R \) fails symmetry, since \( |a-b| \) and \( |b-a| \) can be different values
\( R \) satisfies all three properties, so it is an equivalence relation
\( R \) fails transitivity — for example, \( |0-2|\le 2 \) and \( |2-4|\le 2 \) both hold, but \( |0-4|=4 \not\le 2 \)
questions.explanation:
Reflexive: \( |a-a|=0\le 2 \) always. Symmetric: \( |a-b|=|b-a| \) always.

Transitive fails: \( |0-2|=2\le2 \) and \( |2-4|=2\le2 \), but \( |0-4|=4 \not\le 2 \). So \( R \) is not an equivalence relation.
questions.hint: Check reflexivity and symmetry from the formula directly, then search for a chain of three integers spaced two apart.
distractor_logic: \( |a-a|=0 \), and \( 0\le 2 \) is true for every integer \( a \); reflexivity does in fact hold here.
Absolute value is always symmetric in its two arguments, \( |a-b|=|b-a| \), identically for every \( a,b \); symmetry does hold here.
This overlooks the chain \( 0,2,4 \): \( 0 \) and \( 2 \) are related, \( 2 \) and \( 4 \) are related, but \( 0 \) and \( 4 \) are not, which is a direct failure of transitivity.
mixed_topics: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive

questions.question: Using the operation \( * \) on \( A=\{1,a,b,c\} \) (with \( 1 \) as identity, and every element self-inverse, i.e. \( x*x=1 \) for all \( x \in A \)), define \( x R y \) iff \( x*y=1 \). Confirm \( R \) is an equivalence relation and describe its classes.
options: Since every element is self-inverse, \( x*y=1 \) exactly when \( y=x \), so \( R \) is simply equality on \( A \), giving four singleton classes: \( \{1\},\{a\},\{b\},\{c\} \)
\( R \) groups elements into two classes, since the table has \( 4 \) elements arranged in pairs
\( R \) is not reflexive, since \( 1*1=1 \) is the only case where an element relates to itself
\( R \) is symmetric but not transitive, since \( a*b=c \ne 1 \)
questions.explanation:
Because \( x*x=1 \) for every \( x \in A \), and the table shows no other pair multiplies to \( 1 \) (e.g. \( a*b=c\ne1 \)), \( x*y=1 \) holds exactly when \( y=x \).

So \( R \) is ordinary equality on \( A \), which is trivially reflexive, symmetric and transitive, with four singleton classes.
questions.hint: Since every element is its own inverse, work out exactly which pairs \( (x,y) \) satisfy \( x*y=1 \).
distractor_logic: There is no such pairing here; since every element is its own inverse, \( x*y=1 \) only when \( y \) equals \( x \) itself, giving four separate singleton classes rather than two paired ones.
Every element satisfies \( x*x=1 \) by the given self-inverse property, not just \( 1 \); so \( (x,x)\in R \) for every \( x\in A \), and reflexivity holds fully.
The computation \( a*b=c \) simply means \( (a,b) \notin R \); it says nothing about transitivity of \( R \), which is determined entirely by which pairs do satisfy \( x*y=1 \).

questions.question: On \( \mathbb{N} \), define \( a R b \) iff \( a \) and \( b \) have the same parity (both even or both odd), and let \( f(x)=x+2 \). Given \( a R b \), does \( f(a) R f(b) \) always hold?
options: No, since adding \( 2 \) can turn an even number into an odd number
Yes — adding \( 2 \) never changes whether a number is even or odd, so \( f(a) \) and \( f(b) \) always keep the same parity as \( a \) and \( b \)
Only when \( a \) and \( b \) are both even, not when both are odd
Cannot be determined without knowing whether \( f \) is one-one
questions.explanation:
If \( a \) is even, \( f(a)=a+2 \) is even; if \( a \) is odd, \( f(a)=a+2 \) is odd. The same holds for \( b \).

So if \( a \) and \( b \) share a parity, \( f(a) \) and \( f(b) \) share the same parity too, meaning \( f(a) R f(b) \) always holds.
questions.hint: Check what adding \( 2 \) does to the parity of a single even number and a single odd number.
distractor_logic: Adding an even number such as \( 2 \) always preserves parity: an even number plus \( 2 \) stays even, and an odd number plus \( 2 \) stays odd.
Parity is preserved under adding \( 2 \) uniformly, regardless of whether the starting numbers were both even or both odd; there is no asymmetry between the two cases.
Injectivity of \( f \) is irrelevant here; the preservation of parity under \( f(x)=x+2 \) can be checked directly and does not depend on whether \( f \) is one-one.
mixed_topics: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: Let \( f(x)=x^2+2x \) with domain restricted to \( [-1,\infty) \) and codomain \( [-1,\infty) \). Confirm \( f \) is bijective on this restricted domain, and find \( f^{-1}(x) \).
options: \( f \) is not one-one even after restriction, since \( x^2 \) terms are always non-injective
\( f \) is bijective here (completing the square, \( f(x)=(x+1)^2-1 \) is increasing for \( x\ge -1 \)), and \( f^{-1}(x)=\sqrt{x+1}-1 \)
questions.explanation:
\( f(x)=(x+1)^2-1 \), which is strictly increasing for \( x\ge -1 \), hence one-one; its range is \( [-1,\infty) \), matching the codomain, so \( f \) is onto too.

Setting \( y=(x+1)^2-1 \): \( y+1=(x+1)^2 \), so \( x+1=\sqrt{y+1} \) (taking the non-negative root since \( x\ge -1 \)), giving \( x=\sqrt{y+1}-1 \). So \( f^{-1}(x)=\sqrt{x+1}-1 \).
questions.hint: Complete the square first: \( f(x)=(x+1)^2-1 \). Then set \( y=(x+1)^2-1 \) and solve for \( x \), keeping the positive root since \( x\ge -1 \).
distractor_logic: This has the wrong signs; substituting back does not undo the completed-square shift correctly and fails to return \( x \).
Restricting to \( x\ge -1 \) removes the symmetric branch of the parabola, leaving only the strictly increasing branch, which is genuinely one-one.
This is the reciprocal \( \dfrac{1}{f(x)} \), a completely different quantity from the true inverse function.
mixed_topics: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: Let \( f(x)=\dfrac{1}{1-x} \), with domain \( \mathbb{R}\setminus\{1\} \). Compute \( (f\circ f\circ f)(x) \).
options: \( x \) — that is, \( f\circ f\circ f \) is the identity function
questions.explanation:
\( f(f(x)) = \dfrac{1}{1-\frac{1}{1-x}} = \dfrac{1-x}{(1-x)-1} = \dfrac{1-x}{-x} = \dfrac{x-1}{x} \).

\( f(f(f(x))) = \dfrac{1}{1-\frac{x-1}{x}} = \dfrac{x}{x-(x-1)} = \dfrac{x}{1} = x \).

Checking numerically at \( x=2 \): \( f(2)=-1 \), \( f(-1)=\tfrac{1}{2} \), \( f(\tfrac{1}{2})=2 \), confirming the cycle returns to \( x \).
questions.hint: Compute \( f(f(x)) \) first, simplify fully, then apply \( f \) once more to that simplified result.
distractor_logic: This is only \( (f\circ f)(x) \), one composition short of the full triple composition asked for.
This comes from cubing \( f(x) \) directly, rather than composing \( f \) with itself three times.
This incorrectly treats repeated composition as simply repeating the denominator's expression, rather than substituting each output back into \( f \) in turn.
mixed_topics: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions

questions.question: Define \( f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} \) by \( f(1)=1,\ f(2)=1,\ f(3)=2,\ f(4)=2,\ f(5)=3,\ f(6)=3 \), and so on, with each output value taken by exactly two consecutive inputs. Is \( f \) one-one? Is \( f \) onto?
options: \( f \) is onto (every natural number appears as an output) but not one-one (e.g. \( f(1)=f(2)=1 \))
\( f \) is one-one but not onto, since consecutive inputs never repeat an output
\( f \) is neither one-one nor onto, since repeated outputs always block every codomain value from being reached
\( f \) is bijective, since every natural number has a well-defined image under \( f \)
questions.explanation:
\( f(1)=f(2)=1 \), so two different inputs share the same output — \( f \) is not one-one.

Every natural number \( n \) appears as \( f(2n-1) \) or \( f(2n) \), so every element of the codomain is hit — \( f \) is onto.
questions.hint: Check whether any two different inputs share an output, then check whether every natural number appears somewhere in the output list.
distractor_logic: This reverses the actual behavior; inputs \( 1 \) and \( 2 \) do share the same output \( 1 \), which is exactly why \( f \) fails to be one-one.
Even though outputs repeat, every natural number in the codomain is still eventually reached by some input, since the pattern continues indefinitely; onto does hold.
Having a well-defined image for every input only confirms \( f \) is a valid function; it says nothing about one-oneness, which fails here since some outputs repeat.
mixed_topics: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: Let \( f(x)=x+2 \) and \( g(x)=3x \), both bijections on \( \mathbb{R} \). Verify that \( (g\circ f)^{-1}(x) = (f^{-1}\circ g^{-1})(x) \).
options: \( (g\circ f)^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x-6}{3} \), but \( (f^{-1}\circ g^{-1})(x) = \dfrac{x}{3}-2 \), so the two sides are actually different expressions
Both sides equal \( \dfrac{x-6}{3} \): directly inverting \( g\circ f \) gives \( \dfrac{x-6}{3} \), and computing \( f^{-1}(g^{-1}(x)) = \dfrac{x}{3}-2 = \dfrac{x-6}{3} \) gives the same result
\( (g\circ f)^{-1}(x) = (g^{-1}\circ f^{-1})(x) \), reversing the inverses in the same order as the original composition
Since \( f \) and \( g \) are both bijective, any composition of their inverses automatically equals \( (g\circ f)^{-1} \), regardless of order
questions.explanation:
\( (g\circ f)(x) = 3(x+2) = 3x+6 \). Solving \( y=3x+6 \) for \( x \) gives \( (g\circ f)^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x-6}{3} \).

\( f^{-1}(x)=x-2 \), \( g^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{x}{3} \), so \( (f^{-1}\circ g^{-1})(x) = f^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right) = \dfrac{x}{3}-2 = \dfrac{x-6}{3} \), matching the direct computation exactly.
questions.hint: Find \( (g\circ f)(x) \) first and invert it directly; separately compute \( f^{-1} \) and \( g^{-1} \) and compose them in the order \( f^{-1}\circ g^{-1} \).
distractor_logic: These are in fact the same expression once simplified, since \( \dfrac{x}{3}-2 = \dfrac{x-6}{3} \); this option stops short of simplifying and wrongly treats them as unequal.
This reverses the correct rule; inverting a composition swaps the order of the two inverse functions, it does not keep the original order.
Order matters in general; only the specific order \( f^{-1}\circ g^{-1} \) gives the correct inverse of \( g\circ f \), not \( g^{-1}\circ f^{-1} \).
mixed_topics: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: For each nonzero real \( a \), define \( f_a(x)=ax \). Composing \( f_a \) and \( f_b \) corresponds to which binary operation on the constants \( a \) and \( b \)?
options: \( (f_a\circ f_b)(x) = f_{a+b}(x) \), so composition corresponds to ordinary addition of the constants
Composition of \( f_a \) and \( f_b \) does not correspond to any single binary operation on \( a \) and \( b \), since the result depends on \( x \) too
\( (f_a\circ f_b)(x) = f_{ab}(x) \), so composition of these functions corresponds exactly to ordinary multiplication \( a * b = ab \) on the constants
\( (f_a\circ f_b)(x) = f_{ab}(x) \), but the order of composition still matters, i.e. \( f_a\circ f_b \ne f_b\circ f_a \) in general
questions.explanation:
\( (f_a\circ f_b)(x) = f_a(bx) = a(bx) = (ab)x = f_{ab}(x) \).

So composing \( f_a \) and \( f_b \) always produces \( f_{ab} \), exactly matching ordinary multiplication \( a*b=ab \) on the constants; checking the reverse order gives the same result, since \( f_b(f_a(x))=b(ax)=abx \) too.
questions.hint: Compute \( f_a(f_b(x)) \) directly and compare the resulting coefficient of \( x \) with \( f_{ab}(x) \).
distractor_logic: Checking directly, \( f_a(f_b(x))=a(bx)=abx \), matching \( f_{ab}(x) \), not \( (a+b)x \).
The result \( abx \) equals \( f_{ab}(x) \) exactly, for every \( x \); it corresponds to the single fixed operation \( ab \), independent of which \( x \) is substituted.
Checking directly, \( f_b(f_a(x))=b(ax)=abx=f_{ab}(x) \) also, so in this particular family the order of composition does not matter, since ordinary multiplication of the constants is commutative.
mixed_topics: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions

questions.question: Define \( a*b=a-b \). Is \( * \) a valid binary operation on \( \mathbb{N} \) (i.e. does it satisfy \( * : \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} \))?
options: Yes, since subtraction is a standard, well-defined arithmetic operation
Yes, as long as \( a \) and \( b \) are both natural numbers, their difference is automatically a natural number too
No, because subtraction is never a valid binary operation on any set of numbers
No — for example, \( 2*5=2-5=-3 \), which is not a natural number, so \( * \) is not closed on \( \mathbb{N} \)
questions.explanation:
For a binary operation on \( \mathbb{N} \), every result of \( a*b \) must itself lie in \( \mathbb{N} \).

Taking \( a=2,b=5 \): \( 2*5=2-5=-3 \), which is not a natural number. So \( * \) fails closure and is not a valid binary operation on \( \mathbb{N} \) (though it is perfectly valid on \( \mathbb{Z} \)).
questions.hint: Try a pair where the second number is larger than the first, and check whether the result still lies in \( \mathbb{N} \).
distractor_logic: Being well-defined as ordinary arithmetic does not guarantee the result stays inside \( \mathbb{N} \); closure into the same set is a separate requirement that fails here.
This is false whenever \( b>a \); the difference is then negative, which lies outside \( \mathbb{N} \), exactly as the counterexample \( 2-5=-3 \) shows.

Subtraction is perfectly valid as a binary operation on sets like \( \mathbb{Z} \) or \( \mathbb{R} \), where negative results remain within the set; the failure here is specific to the restricted set \( \mathbb{N} \), not a universal fact about subtraction.

questions.question: On \( \mathbb{R} \), define \( a R b \) iff \( a^4=b^4 \). Find \( [2] \) and \( [0] \).
options: \( [2]=\{2,-2,2i,-2i\} \), including complex fourth roots
\( [0]=\{0,1,-1\} \), since small numbers near zero also satisfy the condition approximately
questions.explanation:
\( x^4=16 \) has real solutions \( x=2 \) and \( x=-2 \), since \( a^4=b^4 \) is equivalent to \( |a|=|b| \) for reals.

\( x^4=0 \) has only the solution \( x=0 \), since a real fourth power is zero only when the base itself is zero. So \( [2]=\{2,-2\} \) and \( [0]=\{0\} \).
questions.hint: Solve \( x^4=2^4 \) and \( x^4=0^4 \) exactly over the real numbers.
distractor_logic: This misses \( -2 \), which also satisfies \( (-2)^4=16=2^4 \), so it belongs in \( [2] \) alongside \( 2 \).
The relation is defined on \( \mathbb{R} \), not \( \mathbb{C} \), so only real solutions belong to the equivalence class; complex roots are outside the set under consideration.
Satisfying an equality only approximately is not the same as satisfying it exactly; only \( a=0 \) gives \( a^4=0\) exactly, since \( 1^4=1\ne0 \).

questions.question: Let \( f(x)=\dfrac{2x-1}{x-3} \), with domain \( \mathbb{R}\setminus\{3\} \). Find the codomain on which \( f \) becomes onto, and give \( f^{-1}(x) \).
options: \( f \) is bijective onto all of \( \mathbb{R} \), with \( f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{3x-1}{x-2} \)
\( f \) is bijective onto \( \mathbb{R}\setminus\{2\} \), with \( f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{3x-1}{x-2} \)
\( f \) is bijective onto \( \mathbb{R}\setminus\{2\} \), with \( f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x-3}{2x-1} \)
\( f \) is bijective onto \( \mathbb{R}\setminus\{3\} \), with \( f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{3x-1}{x-2} \)
questions.explanation:
\( y(x-3)=2x-1 \implies yx-3y=2x-1 \implies x(y-2)=3y-1 \implies x=\dfrac{3y-1}{y-2} \), valid only when \( y \ne 2 \).

So \( f \) is bijective onto \( \mathbb{R}\setminus\{2\} \), and \( f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{3x-1}{x-2} \).
questions.hint: Set \( y=\dfrac{2x-1}{x-3} \) and solve for \( x \) in terms of \( y \); note which value of \( y \) makes the solution impossible.
distractor_logic: This misses that \( y=2 \) has no valid \( x \); solving \( y=f(x) \) for \( y=2 \) leads to a contradiction, so \( 2 \) must be excluded from the codomain.
This simply flips the original fraction upside down, rather than solving \( y=f(x) \) for \( x \) properly.

The excluded codomain value comes from the coefficient structure of \( f \) itself (namely \( y=2 \)), not from the excluded domain value \( 3 \); these two exclusions play different roles and should not be confused.
mixed_topics: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions

questions.question: On \( \mathbb{Z} \), define \( a*b=\max(a,b) \), and let \( a R b \) iff \( a*b=b \). Which of the three defining properties does \( R \) satisfy?
options: \( R \) is symmetric, since \( \max(a,b)=\max(b,a) \) always
\( R \) is not reflexive, since \( a*a=a \) does not equal \( a \) in general
\( R \) is reflexive and transitive (since \( a*b=b \) is equivalent to \( a\le b \), the usual order relation), but not symmetric
\( R \) is an equivalence relation, since it is built directly from a well-defined binary operation
questions.explanation:
\( a*b=\max(a,b)=b \) exactly when \( a\le b \).

Reflexive: \( a\le a \) always. Transitive: \( a\le b \) and \( b\le c \) give \( a\le c \). Symmetric fails: \( a\le b \) does not imply \( b\le a \) unless \( a=b \).
questions.hint: Rewrite the condition \( a*b=b \) as an ordinary inequality on \( a \) and \( b \), then check each property against that inequality.
distractor_logic: This confuses the operation \( * \) being commutative with the relation \( R \) being symmetric; \( a*b=b \) does not generally imply \( b*a=a \).
\( \max(a,a)=a \) always, exactly matching the required value \( a \) itself, so reflexivity does hold for every \( a \).
Being built from a well-defined operation does not guarantee symmetry; here it specifically fails, as \( a*b=b \) means \( a\le b \), which is not a symmetric condition.
mixed_topics: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive

questions.question: On \( \mathbb{Z} \), let \( a R b \) iff \( a \) and \( b \) leave the same remainder modulo \( 3 \) (an equivalence relation with three classes). Let \( f(x)=x+3 \), which is bijective on \( \mathbb{Z} \) with inverse \( f^{-1}(x)=x-3 \). If \( a R b \), do \( f(a) R f(b) \) and \( f^{-1}(a) R f^{-1}(b) \) both hold?
options: Only \( f \) preserves \( R \); \( f^{-1} \) does not, since subtraction can change remainders that addition does not
Neither \( f \) nor \( f^{-1} \) preserves \( R \), since shifting by a constant always changes the remainder
Both preserve \( R \), but only because \( f \) happens to be bijective; a non-bijective function could never preserve \( R \) this way
Yes to both — since \( 3 \equiv 0 \pmod 3 \), adding or subtracting \( 3 \) never changes a number's remainder modulo \( 3 \), so both \( f \) and \( f^{-1} \) preserve \( R \)
questions.explanation:
Since \( 3 \) is itself a multiple of \( 3 \), adding \( 3 \) to any integer leaves its remainder modulo \( 3 \) unchanged, and so does subtracting \( 3 \).

So if \( a \) and \( b \) share a remainder modulo \( 3 \), then \( a+3 \) and \( b+3 \) do too, and likewise for \( a-3 \) and \( b-3 \); both \( f \) and \( f^{-1} \) preserve \( R \).
questions.hint: Check what adding or subtracting \( 3 \) does to a number's remainder when divided by \( 3 \).
distractor_logic: Subtracting \( 3 \) shifts a number by a multiple of \( 3 \) in exactly the same way that adding \( 3 \) does, so remainders modulo \( 3 \) are unaffected either way.

This is false specifically because the shift amount \( 3 \) is itself a multiple of the modulus \( 3 \); a shift by a non-multiple, like \( 1 \) or \( 2 \), would indeed change remainders, but \( 3 \) does not.
Bijectivity is not what causes the preservation here; it comes from the shift amount being a multiple of \( 3 \), and many non-bijective functions could also happen to preserve such a relation.
mixed_topics: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions

questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: On \( \mathbb{N} \), define \( a R b \) iff \( \gcd(a,b) > 1 \). Which property fails for the specific element \( a=1 \), and does \( R \) qualify as an equivalence relation?
options: Reflexivity fails at \( a=1 \), since \( \gcd(1,1)=1 \), which is not greater than \( 1 \); \( R \) is symmetric but not transitive either (e.g. \( 2R6 \) and \( 6R3 \) hold, but \( 2R3 \) fails since \( \gcd(2,3)=1 \)), so \( R \) is not an equivalence relation
\( R \) is reflexive for every \( a \in \mathbb{N} \), since \( \gcd(a,a)=a \) is always at least \( a \)
\( R \) is transitive, since sharing a common factor is naturally an inheritable property
\( R \) is not symmetric, since \( \gcd(a,b) \) and \( \gcd(b,a) \) can give different results
questions.explanation:
\( \gcd(1,1)=1 \), which is not \( >1 \), so reflexivity fails at \( a=1 \) even though it holds for every \( a>1 \).

Symmetry holds since \( \gcd(a,b)=\gcd(b,a) \) always.

Transitivity fails: \( \gcd(2,6)=2>1 \) and \( \gcd(6,3)=3>1 \), but \( \gcd(2,3)=1 \), not \( >1 \). So \( R \) is not an equivalence relation.
questions.hint: Check reflexivity at the specific value \( a=1 \) first, then look for a chain of three numbers that breaks transitivity.
distractor_logic: This overlooks \( a=1 \), where \( \gcd(1,1)=1 \), which fails the strict inequality \( >1 \); reflexivity does not hold universally.
The counterexample \( 2,6,3 \) shows a genuine break: \( 2 \) and \( 6 \) share a factor, \( 6 \) and \( 3 \) share a factor, but \( 2 \) and \( 3 \) share none beyond \( 1 \).
The greatest common divisor is symmetric in its two arguments by definition, so \( \gcd(a,b)=\gcd(b,a)\) always; symmetry does hold for \( R \).

questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: For the operation \( * \) on \( A=\{1,2,3\} \) given by \( 1*1=1,\ 1*2=2,\ 1*3=3,\ 2*1=2,\ 2*2=1,\ 2*3=1,\ 3*1=3,\ 3*2=1,\ 3*3=1 \) (with identity \( e=1 \)), define \( a R b \) iff \( a*b=1 \). Confirm \( R \) is an equivalence relation and find its classes.
options: \( R \) cannot be an equivalence relation, since this operation is not associative
\( R \) is indeed reflexive, symmetric and transitive here — an equivalence relation — with classes \( \{1\} \) and \( \{2,3\} \)
\( R \) is reflexive and symmetric, but fails transitivity, since \( 2R3 \) and \( 3R2 \) hold yet \( 2R2 \) needs separate checking
\( R \) has three separate classes, \( \{1\},\{2\},\{3\} \), since every element is distinct
questions.explanation:
From the table, \( a*b=1 \) exactly for the pairs \( (1,1),(2,2),(2,3),(3,2),(3,3) \).

This set is reflexive (contains \( (1,1),(2,2),(3,3) \)), symmetric (contains both \( (2,3) \) and \( (3,2) \)), and transitive (every required chain closes up). So \( R \) is an equivalence relation with classes \( \{1\} \) and \( \{2,3\} \).
questions.hint: List every pair \( (a,b) \) from the table for which \( a*b=1 \), then check reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity against that list.
distractor_logic: Associativity of \( * \) has no bearing on whether a relation defined from it happens to be reflexive, symmetric and transitive; checking the actual pairs shows all three properties genuinely hold here.
Checking directly, \( 2*2=1 \) does hold, so \( (2,2)\in R \) as well; transitivity does not actually break here.
This misses that \( 2 \) and \( 3 \) are related to each other, since \( 2*3=1 \) and \( 3*2=1 \); they belong together in a single class, not separate ones.

questions.question: On the set of all straight lines in a plane, define \( l_1 R l_2 \) iff \( l_1 \) is parallel to \( l_2 \) (including a line being considered parallel to itself). Confirm \( R \) is an equivalence relation, and describe \( [l] \) for a fixed line \( l \).
options: \( R \) is not reflexive, since a line cannot be considered parallel to itself
\( R \) is reflexive and symmetric, but not transitive, since three lines can form a triangle without being pairwise parallel

\( R \) is an equivalence relation (reflexive by convention, symmetric and transitive by the geometric properties of parallel lines), and \( [l] \) is the set of every line with the same slope as \( l \)
\( [l] \) contains only the line \( l \) itself and no others, since each line has its own unique direction
questions.explanation:
Reflexive by convention: every line is parallel to itself. Symmetric: if \( l_1 \) is parallel to \( l_2 \), then \( l_2 \) is parallel to \( l_1 \). Transitive: lines parallel to a common line are parallel to each other.

So \( R \) is an equivalence relation, and \( [l] \) consists of every line sharing the same slope as \( l \), of which there are infinitely many.
questions.hint: Recall the standard convention that a line is parallel to itself, and think about which lines share a slope.
distractor_logic: By the standard convention used for this relation, a line is taken to be parallel to itself, which is exactly what makes \( R \) reflexive; without this convention \( R \) would not be an equivalence relation at all.

Lines forming a triangle are simply not related by \( R \) in the first place, since they are not pairwise parallel; this is not an actual violation of transitivity among lines that genuinely are pairwise parallel.
Infinitely many distinct lines can share the same slope as \( l \) (for instance, any vertical shift of \( l \)), so \( [l] \) contains far more than just \( l \).

questions.question: On \( \mathbb{R} \), define \( a R b \) iff \( f(a)=f(b) \), where \( f(x)=(x-1)(x-3) \). Find \( [2] \).
options: \( [2]=\{2,4\} \), following the usual pattern where quadratics pair each point with a mirror point
\( [2]=\{1,3\} \), since these are the roots of \( f(x)=0 \)
\( [2] \) cannot be determined without restricting the domain of \( f \), since quadratics are not one-one on \( \mathbb{R} \)
\( [2]=\{2\} \) — since \( f(2)=-1 \) is the minimum value of this upward parabola, achieved uniquely at the vertex \( x=2 \), no other real number shares this output
questions.explanation:
\( f(2)=(2-1)(2-3)=(1)(-1)=-1 \). Solving \( (x-1)(x-3)=-1 \): expand to \( x^2-4x+3=-1 \), so \( x^2-4x+4=0 \), i.e. \( (x-2)^2=0 \).

This has the single repeated root \( x=2 \), since \( x=2 \) is exactly the vertex of the upward parabola \( f \), where the minimum value \( -1 \) is achieved uniquely. So \( [2]=\{2\} \).
questions.hint: Compute \( f(2) \) first, then solve \( f(x)=f(2) \) exactly as a quadratic equation.
distractor_logic: This pattern only applies to points away from the vertex; exactly at the vertex, the mirror point coincides with the point itself, giving a singleton class instead of a genuine pair.
This solves \( f(x)=0 \), not \( f(x)=f(2) \); a completely different equation was solved than the one the question asks about.
Even without any domain restriction, solving \( f(x)=f(2) \) directly and exactly determines \( [2] \); general non-injectivity elsewhere does not prevent computing this specific equivalence class.

questions.topic: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
questions.question: On \( \mathbb{Z} \), define \( a R b \) iff \( a^2+b^2 \) is even. Determine whether \( R \) is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, and identify its equivalence classes if it is an equivalence relation.
options: \( R \) is reflexive, symmetric and transitive (an equivalence relation), and it splits \( \mathbb{Z} \) into exactly two classes — even integers and odd integers — since \( a^2+b^2 \) is even exactly when \( a \) and \( b \) have the same parity
\( R \) is reflexive and symmetric, but fails transitivity, since parity conditions rarely chain together correctly
\( R \) is not reflexive, since \( a^2+a^2=2a^2 \) is only even when \( a \) itself is even
\( R \) splits \( \mathbb{Z} \) into four classes, based on the remainder of \( a \) modulo \( 4 \)
questions.explanation:
\( a^2 \) is even exactly when \( a \) is even, and odd exactly when \( a \) is odd; so \( a^2+b^2 \) is even exactly when \( a \) and \( b \) share the same parity.

Reflexive, symmetric and transitive all follow immediately from this restatement, since "sharing the same parity" is itself an equivalence relation with exactly two classes: even integers and odd integers.
questions.hint: Rewrite the condition in terms of the parity of \( a \) and \( b \) individually, rather than working with \( a^2+b^2 \) directly.
distractor_logic: Checking directly with the sum rule: if \( a^2+b^2 \) and \( b^2+c^2 \) are both even, their total \( a^2+2b^2+c^2 \) is even, and subtracting the even quantity \( 2b^2 \) shows \( a^2+c^2 \) must also be even; transitivity does hold here.
\( 2a^2 \) is always even regardless of whether \( a \) is even or odd, since multiplying any integer by \( 2 \) always produces an even result.

The defining condition only distinguishes even from odd, not finer remainders modulo \( 4 \); for instance \( 1 \) and \( 5 \) are both odd with different remainders mod \( 4 \), yet they land in the same class here.

questions.question: Let \( f(x)=|x-2| \), with domain restricted to \( [2,\infty) \). Confirm \( f \) is bijective on this restricted domain (with codomain \( [0,\infty) \)), and find \( f^{-1}(x) \).
options: \( f \) is still not one-one even after restriction, since absolute value functions are never one-one
On \( [2,\infty) \), \( f(x)=x-2 \) (since \( x\ge 2 \) makes \( x-2\ge 0 \)), which is bijective onto \( [0,\infty) \), with \( f^{-1}(x)=x+2 \)
questions.explanation:
Since \( x\ge2 \), \( x-2\ge0 \), so \( f(x)=|x-2|=x-2 \) on this domain, which is strictly increasing and hence one-one, with range \( [0,\infty) \), matching the codomain.

Solving \( y=x-2 \) for \( x \) gives \( x=y+2 \), so \( f^{-1}(x)=x+2 \).
questions.hint: Simplify \( |x-2| \) using the fact that \( x-2\ge0 \) throughout the restricted domain, then invert the resulting linear expression.
distractor_logic: Restricting the domain to \( x\ge 2 \) removes the branch where \( x<2 \), leaving only the increasing branch \( x-2 \), which is genuinely one-one.

Carrying the absolute value into the inverse is unnecessary; once restricted to \( x\ge2 \), \( f(x) \) simplifies to the linear expression \( x-2 \), whose inverse is simply \( x+2 \) with no absolute value needed.
This has the wrong sign; substituting back, \( f(2-x)=|2-x-2|=|-x|=|x| \), which does not return \( x \) in general, for instance it fails for negative \( x \).

questions.question: Let \( f:\{1,2,3,4\}\to\{1,2,3\} \) be given by \( f(1)=1,\ f(2)=2,\ f(3)=2,\ f(4)=3 \). Is \( f \) invertible?
options: Yes, since every element of the codomain has at least one preimage, which is enough to guarantee an inverse
Yes, and \( f^{-1}(2) = \{2,3\} \), since inverses can map to a set of values when needed
No — \( f \) is onto (every element of \( \{1,2,3\} \) is hit) but not one-one (\( f(2)=f(3)=2 \)), and invertibility requires bijectivity, so \( f^{-1} \) does not exist
No, because \( f \) is neither one-one nor onto
questions.explanation:
Every element of \( \{1,2,3\} \) appears as some \( f(x) \), so \( f \) is onto.

But \( f(2)=2=f(3) \), so two different inputs share an output — \( f \) is not one-one. Since invertibility requires both properties together, \( f^{-1} \) does not exist.
questions.hint: Check whether every codomain element is hit (onto), and separately whether any two inputs share an output (one-one).
distractor_logic: Onto alone is not sufficient for invertibility; \( f \) must also be one-one, which fails here since two different inputs, \( 2 \) and \( 3 \), share the same output.
A genuine inverse function must assign a single, unique output to each input; being forced to map \( 2 \) to a set of two values is precisely why \( f \) is not invertible in the first place.
\( f \) actually is onto, since the codomain \( \{1,2,3\} \) is fully covered by some input; only the one-one property fails here.

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: Let \( f(x)=\sqrt{x} \) (domain \( [0,\infty) \)) and \( g(x)=x-4 \) (domain \( \mathbb{R} \)). What is the domain of \( (f\circ g)(x) \)?
options: \( \mathbb{R} \), since \( g \) itself is defined for every real number
\( [0,\infty) \), since this is the domain of \( f \) and the composition inherits it directly
\( (-\infty,4] \), since \( x-4 \) must stay negative or zero for the square root to be defined
\( [4,\infty) \) — since \( f \) requires its input to be \( \ge 0 \), we need \( g(x)=x-4\ge 0 \), i.e. \( x\ge 4 \)
questions.explanation:
\( f \) is only defined when its input is \( \ge 0 \), so \( (f\circ g)(x)=\sqrt{g(x)}=\sqrt{x-4} \) requires \( x-4\ge0 \), i.e. \( x\ge4 \).

So the domain of \( f\circ g \) is \( [4,\infty) \), which is narrower than the domain of \( g \) alone.
questions.hint: Write down the condition that \( f \) needs its input to satisfy, then apply that condition to \( g(x) \) instead of to \( x \) directly.
distractor_logic: The domain of the composition is governed by the requirement that the output of \( g \) must be a valid input for \( f \), not merely by the domain of \( g \) alone; \( f \) itself only accepts non-negative inputs.
The composition's domain is restricted by which \( x \) values make \( g(x) \) fall inside \( f \)'s domain, which works out to \( x\ge4 \), not simply \( f \)'s own domain taken at face value.
This has the inequality direction backwards; a square root requires its argument to be non-negative, \( \ge 0 \), not non-positive, so \( g(x)=x-4\ge0 \) gives \( x\ge4 \), not \( x\le4 \).

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: Under composition of functions on \( \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} \), the identity function \( \text{id}(x)=x \) plays a role analogous to which concept from binary operations, and why?
options: It plays the role of the identity element \( e \), since for every function \( f \), \( f\circ\text{id} = \text{id}\circ f = f \), exactly matching the requirement \( a*e=e*a=a \)
It plays the role of the inverse element, since composing any function with \( \text{id} \) always undoes that function completely
It has no analogous role, since function composition and binary operations are unrelated concepts
It plays the role of the identity element, but only on the left, i.e. only \( \text{id}\circ f = f \) holds, not \( f\circ\text{id}=f \)
questions.explanation:
\( (f\circ\text{id})(x) = f(\text{id}(x)) = f(x) \), and \( (\text{id}\circ f)(x) = \text{id}(f(x)) = f(x) \).

Both orders return \( f \) unchanged, exactly matching the two-sided identity requirement \( a*e=e*a=a \) from binary operations, with composition playing the role of \( * \) and \( \text{id} \) playing the role of \( e \).
questions.hint: Recall the binary-operation identity requirement \( a*e=e*a=a \), and check whether composing with \( \text{id} \) matches it on both sides.
distractor_logic: Composing with \( \text{id} \) leaves \( f \) completely unchanged; it does not undo or cancel \( f \) in any way. Undoing \( f \) is instead the role played by \( f^{-1} \), a different function entirely.
Composition of functions is itself a binary operation on the set of functions, so identity-element reasoning applies directly and meaningfully here.

Checking directly, both orders give back \( f \) unchanged: \( (f\circ\text{id})(x)=f(\text{id}(x))=f(x) \) and \( (\text{id}\circ f)(x)=\text{id}(f(x))=f(x) \); the identity behavior holds on both sides.

questions.topic: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
questions.question: For which linear functions \( f(x)=ax+b \) (\( a\ne0 \)) does \( f=f^{-1} \), i.e. \( f(f(x))=x \) for every \( x \)?
options: Only \( f(x)=x \) satisfies this, since a function can only be its own inverse if it changes nothing at all
Either \( f(x)=x \) (i.e. \( a=1,b=0 \)), or \( f(x)=-x+b \) for any real \( b \) (i.e. \( a=-1 \), \( b \) arbitrary) — both families satisfy \( f(f(x))=x \)
Only functions with \( b=0 \) satisfy this, regardless of the value of \( a \)
No linear function other than the identity can ever equal its own inverse
questions.explanation:
\( f(f(x)) = a(ax+b)+b = a^2x+ab+b \). Matching this to \( x \) requires \( a^2=1 \) and \( ab+b=0 \), i.e. \( b(a+1)=0 \).

If \( a=1 \): \( 2b=0 \), so \( b=0 \), giving only \( f(x)=x \). If \( a=-1 \): \( b(0)=0 \) automatically, so any \( b \) works, giving the whole family \( f(x)=-x+b \).
questions.hint: Expand \( f(f(x))=a(ax+b)+b \) fully, then match coefficients of \( x \) and the constant term against the target expression \( x \).
distractor_logic: Checking directly, \( f(x)=-x+b \) also satisfies \( f(f(x))=-(-x+b)+b=x \) for any \( b \), so plenty of non-trivial self-inverse linear functions exist beyond the identity.
Checking directly with \( a=1,b=5 \): \( f(f(x))=1(x+5)+5=x+10\ne x \), so this family fails; the correct condition requires \( a=\pm1 \), and when \( a=-1 \), any \( b \) works, not only \( b=0 \).
This is contradicted directly by \( f(x)=-x+b \), which composes with itself to give back \( x \) for every real \( b \), as a straightforward substitution confirms.

topics.name: Types of Relations — Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
topics.summary: A relation \( R \) on a set \( A \) is any subset of \( A \times A \), written \( R \subseteq A \times A \). Three properties describe how a relation behaves: reflexive, where \( \forall a \in A,\ (a, a) \in R \); symmetric, where \( (a, b) \in R \implies (b, a) \in R \); and transitive, where \( (a, b) \text{ and } (b, c) \in R \implies (a, c) \in R \). Each property must be checked independently across every relevant element or pair \— no property can be assumed from the others. A relation defined by an explicit list of pairs is checked directly against that list; a relation defined by a condition on \( \mathbb{N}, \mathbb{Z} \) or \( \mathbb{R} \) is checked by testing the condition algebraically, always against a clearly stated underlying set. Many familiar relations \— divisibility, inequalities, distance conditions \— satisfy only some of the three properties, and finding a single counterexample is enough to rule one out.
key_formulas: Transitive: \( (a, b) \text{ and } (b, c) \in R \implies (a, c) \in R \)
topics.worked_example: On \( \mathbb{Z} \), let \( R = \{(a,b) : a-b \text{ is even}\} \). Reflexive: \( a-a=0 \) is even, so \( (a,a)\in R \) for every \( a \). Symmetric: if \( a-b \) is even, so is \( b-a=-(a-b) \). Transitive: if \( a-b \) and \( b-c \) are both even, their sum \( a-c \) is even too. All three hold, so \( R \) is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
common_mistakes: Checking reflexivity, symmetry or transitivity on only a few elements or pairs instead of confirming the property holds for every single one
Assuming that any two of the three properties automatically imply the third
Leaving the underlying set unstated for a condition-based relation, making reflexivity or symmetry impossible to verify precisely

topics.name: Equivalence Relations and Equivalence Classes
topics.summary: An equivalence relation is a relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive all at once \— the conjunction of all three, never assumed from just one or two. Equivalence relations partition their underlying set into disjoint equivalence classes, where the class of an element \( a \) is \( [a] = \{x \in A : (x, a) \in R\} \). Every element of \( A \) belongs to exactly one class, and two elements share a class exactly when they are related. A very common source of equivalence relations is the kernel of a function: defining \( a R b \) iff \( f(a)=f(b) \) for any function \( f \) always produces an equivalence relation, since it directly inherits reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity from ordinary equality. Classic examples include congruence modulo \( n \) on \( \mathbb{Z} \), and "having the same remainder" or "being parallel" style relations, each of which partitions its set into a small, well-understood number of classes.
key_formulas: Kernel relation: \( a R b \iff f(a) = f(b) \) is always an equivalence relation
topics.worked_example: On \( \mathbb{Z} \), let \( a R b \) iff \( a \equiv b \pmod 5 \). This is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, so it is an equivalence relation. The equivalence class \( [2] \) is the set of all integers leaving remainder \( 2 \) on division by \( 5 \), i.e. \( [2] = \{\ldots,-8,-3,2,7,12,\ldots\} \), and there are exactly \( 5 \) such classes in total, one for each possible remainder \( 0,1,2,3,4 \).
common_mistakes: Declaring a relation an equivalence relation after checking only two of the three properties
Listing only a few elements of an equivalence class instead of describing the class completely
Confusing the number of equivalence classes with the number of elements in the underlying set

topics.name: One-One and Onto Functions
topics.summary: A function \( f : A \to B \) is one-one (injective) when \( f(x_1) = f(x_2) \implies x_1 = x_2 \), meaning distinct inputs always give distinct outputs. It is onto (surjective) when \( \forall y \in B,\ \exists x \in A \text{ such that } f(x) = y \), meaning every element of the codomain is actually reached. A function that is both one-one and onto is bijective \— again a conjunction that must be checked as two separate conditions, since a function can easily satisfy one without the other. Whether a given rule defines a one-one or onto function depends heavily on the stated domain and codomain: \( f(x)=x^2 \) is neither one-one nor onto on \( \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} \), yet becomes bijective once the domain and codomain are both restricted to \( [0,\infty) \). This restriction technique \— narrowing the domain to remove repeated outputs, and narrowing the codomain to match the actual range \— is the standard way to turn a non-bijective rule into a bijective one.
key_formulas: Onto: \( \forall y \in B,\ \exists x \in A \text{ such that } f(x) = y \)
topics.worked_example: Let \( f(x)=x^2 \), \( f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} \). This is not one-one, since \( f(2)=f(-2)=4 \) with \( 2 \ne -2 \), and not onto, since no real \( x \) gives \( f(x)=-1 \). Restricting to \( f:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty) \), the negative branch is removed (making it one-one) and the codomain exactly matches the range (making it onto), so this restricted version is bijective.
common_mistakes: Treating a function with all distinct outputs on a small sample as automatically one-one everywhere
Assuming a function that hits every codomain value at least once must also be one-one
Forgetting to restrict both the domain and the codomain when turning a non-bijective rule into a bijective one

topics.name: Composition of Functions and Invertible Functions
topics.summary: The composition of two functions is written \( (g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x)) \), always applying \( f \) first and \( g \) second, read right-to-left. Composition is generally not commutative: \( (g\circ f)(x) \) and \( (f\circ g)(x) \) are usually different functions. An inverse function \( f^{-1} \) exists only once \( f \) has been confirmed bijective, and it must never be confused with the reciprocal \( \dfrac{1}{f(x)} \) \— these are entirely different objects, one reversing the rule of \( f \) and the other dividing by its output. Finding \( f^{-1} \) algebraically means setting \( y=f(x) \) and solving for \( x \) in terms of \( y \). Composition and inversion interact predictably: composing a function with its own inverse (in either order) always returns the identity, and inverting a composition reverses both the functions and their order, i.e. \( (g\circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1}\circ g^{-1} \).
key_formulas: \( f^{-1} \) exists only when \( f \) is bijective
topics.worked_example: Let \( f(x)=2x+3 \) and \( g(x)=x-1 \). Then \( (g\circ f)(x)=g(2x+3)=2x+2 \), while \( (f\circ g)(x)=f(x-1)=2x+1 \) \— different functions, confirming composition order matters. Since \( f \) is bijective, setting \( y=2x+3 \) and solving gives \( f^{-1}(x)=\dfrac{x-3}{2} \), which is not the same as \( \dfrac{1}{2x+3} \).
common_mistakes: Reversing the order of composition, computing \( f(g(x)) \) when \( (g\circ f)(x) \) was asked, or vice versa
Declaring a function invertible without first confirming it is bijective on its stated domain and codomain

topics.name: Binary Operations
topics.summary: A binary operation on a set \( A \) is a rule \( * : A \times A \to A \) that combines any two elements \( a, b \in A \) into a result \( a * b \), which must itself always lie in \( A \) \— this closure requirement is easy to overlook when an operation is only valid on a larger set. An identity element \( e \) satisfies \( a * e = e * a = a \) for every \( a \), and an inverse of \( a \) satisfies \( a * a^{-1} = a^{-1} * a = e \) \— both must be checked on both sides, since a non-commutative operation can have a one-sided identity or inverse that fails on the other side. Commutativity (\( a*b=b*a \)) and associativity (\( (a*b)*c = a*(b*c) \)) are independent properties: neither implies the other, and small Cayley tables are the standard way to check both, along with identity and inverse elements, by direct inspection of table entries.
key_formulas: Identity: \( a * e = e * a = a \)
topics.worked_example: On \( \mathbb{Z} \), define \( a*b=a+b-ab \). Testing associativity: \( (a*b)*c \) and \( a*(b*c) \) both expand to \( a+b+c-ab-bc-ca+abc \), so \( * \) is associative; it is also commutative since \( a+b-ab=b+a-ba \). The identity is \( e=0 \), since \( a*0=a+0-0=a \) and \( 0*a=a \) as well, checked on both sides.
common_mistakes: Assuming an operation is closed on a subset without checking that every result stays inside that subset
Checking an identity or inverse element on only one side instead of both
Assuming commutativity implies associativity, or the reverse
